items.title: SIMA 2026 : le ministre Bacary Sarr clôture le salon et veut en faire un rendez-vous diplomatique du Sénégal
items.description: Le ministre de la Communication et des Relations avec les Institutions a refermé, à Dakar, la deuxième édition du Salon International des Médias d'Afrique. Il y a réaffirmé l'ambition du Sénégal d'ancrer l'événement dans la durée. Après trois jours d'échanges (8-10 octobre 2026), c'est le Dr Bacary Sarr qui a baissé le rideau sur la deuxième édition du Salon International des Médias d'Afrique (SIMA). Le ministre de la Communication et des Relations avec les Institutions a présidé la cérémonie de clôture, au Grand Théâtre National Doudou Ndiaye Rose, où le salon se tenait du 8 au 10 octobre autour du thème « Bâtir un écosystème médiatique souverain et performant en Afrique ». Mobilisation panafricaine Le ministre a d'abord souligné la forte participation venue de tout le continent. Professionnels des médias, experts, institutions et partenaires du Sénégal, de plusieurs pays africains et d'autres régions du monde avaient fait le déplacement pour débattre de l'avenir du paysage médiatique. Dr Bacary Sarr a également salué la contribution des deux pays invités d'honneur, la République fédérale d'Allemagne et l'Algérie. Selon le communiqué du ministère, leur présence a illustré la vocation du SIMA à favoriser le dialogue, le partage d'expériences et la coopération médiatique entre l'Afrique et ses partenaires. Le SIMA, un outil d'influence pour le Sénégal C'est sur l'avenir du salon que le ministre s'est montré le plus clair. Il a réaffirmé l'ambition du Sénégal d'inscrire durablement le SIMA dans son agenda diplomatique, afin d'en faire un rendez-vous régulier de dialogue, de coopération et d'influence au service des médias africains. Pour Dakar, l'événement ne doit donc pas rester une manifestation ponctuelle, mais devenir un levier de rayonnement. Sous l'œil du ministre, les participants ont abordé la régulation et l'autorégulation des médias, les modèles économiques, la lutte contre la désinformation, les industries créatives, le leadership féminin, la liberté de la presse et la souveraineté narrative. L'intelligence artificielle a occupé une place à part. Elle représente, d'après le ministère, à la fois une opportunité pour les médias et un défi majeur pour la fiabilité de l'information, avec de nouvelles formes de désinformation à combattre. En fin de cérémonie, Dr Bacary Sarr a remercié les partenaires, le Comité de pilotage, le Comité scientifique et la Maison de la Presse, ainsi que les professionnels, intervenants et équipes mobilisés pour la réussite de cette édition. O.B.N

items.title: Türkiye: End Internet Censorship
items.description: Click to expand Image Tags, with “Access blocked” and the name of blocked accounts belonging to journalists and media outlets, LGBT and women’s rights groups, and other rights defenders, are tied to the gates of Turkey’s Constitutional Court, to protest the Turkish authorities’ blocking of hundreds of social media accounts and websites. Ankara, October 7, 2026. © 2026 Yıldız Yazıcıoğlu (Istanbul, October 12, 2026) – The Turkish authorities over the last month have substantially escalated internet censorship, Human Rights Watch said today, along with ARTICLE 19, the Freedom of Expression Association, and 18 other organizations. Social media platforms should take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to suppressing independent media and violating the right to freedom of expression. The Turkish authorities should stop issuing blocking orders to restrict content and accounts on social media and websites in violation of the right to freedom of expression. The following is the groups’ statement: ARTICLE 19, Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD), Human Rights Watch, and the undersigned human rights and media freedom organisations are deeply concerned by the severe escalation of internet censorship in Türkiye in the past month. We urge social media platforms to take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to the suppression of independent media and violations of the right to freedom of expression. We call on the Turkish government immediately to cease the use of blocking orders and other restrictive measures that violate the right to freedom of expression, and to ensure that any restrictions on online content fully comply with Türkiye’s obligations under international human rights law. In the month of September 2026 alone, İFÖD documented Turkish authorities and courts ordering the blocking of access to at least 1,270 accounts on the social media platform X, which had a combined following of 35 million. X complied with at least 90 percent of the orders by geo-blocking them (withholding access to them in Türkiye only). In many cases, the accounts were blocked in the context of an ongoing and wide-ranging crackdown on associations and activists defending the rights of LGBTQ+ people. In other cases, the authorities cited unspecified “national security and public order” grounds. Accounts withheld include news outlets such as soL Haber and Mezopotamya Ajansı; rights organisations including Amnesty Türkiye and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA); LGBTQ+; and women’s rights organisations such as Kaos GL and the Federation of Women’s Associations, as well as those of numerous journalists and academics. X also withheld the accounts of İFÖD, its co-founder, Yaman Akdeniz, and its Engelliweb account, which monitors and documents internet censorship in Türkiye. This account plays a critical role in enabling civil society, journalists, and the public to monitor and track websites, social media accounts and content subjected to access restrictions. Blocking T24, one of Türkiye’s biggest and oldest remaining independent news outlets, is particularly troubling. On 29 September, access was blocked to the T24 website and X account with 1.9 million followers, with a court order citing 118 news articles published on the site. The order claimed that the content was “aimed at disrupting and weakening the Turkish family structure” and of a nature “that would adversely affect the developmental process of young and underage individuals concerning sexual orientation and gender identity.” The order cited preventing crime and protecting public order as grounds for the measure but provided no explanation about how the cited content posed a threat to either objective or why blocking an entire news website and social media account was necessary and proportionate. The website has been inaccessible in Türkiye since 30 September. T24 changed its X handle in an attempt to prevent the account from being withheld in Türkiye, then changed it again, after another order blocked access to its second handle. Bianet, another online news outlet which focuses on human rights, also changed its X handle to escape censorship after its account with 400,000 followers was blocked. The court order blocking access to T24 was taken in the context of the “my family is safe” criminal investigations – a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people which targets activists, associations and a journalist advocating for their rights. The websites and social media accounts of at least 96 organizations and individuals were blocked on the same grounds. While most of the cases concern X, Meta has also withheld access to the Instagram and Facebook accounts of several media and civil society organisations, including, Kısa Dalga, Kaos GL, and the Civic Space Studies Association as part of the same operation. Türkiye’s long-standing abuse of Article 8/A of its Internet Law Most of the blocking decisions in September and October invoked Article 8/A of Türkiye’s Internet Law. Article 8/A, used as a tool for internet censorship since its introduction in 2015, provides that online content deemed a threat to national security, public order or presenting a risk on other grounds listed in the article can be removed or blocked on orders of the executive in urgent cases, subject to review later by a Criminal Peace Judgeship, the court assigned such cases. Major examples include blocking access to Wikipedia for 2.5 years in 2017, and to Türkiye’s leading user-generated online discussion platform Ekşi Sözlük for a year in 2023. The Constitutional Court eventually restored both, finding that blocking the entire sites had violated freedom of expression. The use of Article 8/A intensified sharply from 2025, with few safeguards or independent oversight and limited redress for those affected. The Constitutional Court has not ruled on any restrictions under Article 8/A since 2023. Concerning developments aimed at expanding censorship There is no indication that this pressure will ease. On the contrary, the government is taking further measures to accelerate and centralise internet censorship. On 31 July, Law No. 7590 transferred the powers previously exercised by the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA) contained in the Internet Law, to the Cybersecurity Directorate. This includes the authority to block sites on the request of the presidency or relevant ministries based on Article 8/A. This transfer of authority is troubling. The Cybersecurity Directorate is directly attached to the presidency, consolidating executive control over information and serving as the command centre for Türkiye’s censorship regime. Separately, on 24 September, the justice minister announced the establishment of new “Digital Space Security and Countering Disinformation Bureaux,” where specialised public prosecutors will closely monitor “criminal content and activities encouraging crime on digital platforms” including ‘spreading disinformation.” They are tasked in particular with identifying suspects and initiating criminal proceedings to intervene “more swiftly.” Social media platforms should take urgent action to uphold their human rights responsibilities The conduct of social media platforms forms an essential part of internet censorship in Türkiye. In September and early October, account holders reported receiving only a notification from platforms stating that their account had been withheld in Türkiye under Article 8/A, without any reason or explanation why or how the article had been applied. Some were unable to access the underlying blocking orders even after repeatedly requesting them from the platforms. Without access to the orders, users cannot examine the legal basis for the restriction or even identify to which Criminal Judgeship of Peace to submit their objections. Even when users were able to obtain the orders, the orders often failed to identify the specific content allegedly justifying the blocking of the entire account. Neither X nor Meta have provided public explanations about their responses to the September-October censorship waves. Human Rights Watch wrote to the two platforms requesting comment on their compliance with Turkish courts’ recent blocking orders. Neither platform had responded by the time of publication. Under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, companies have a responsibility to respect human rights by avoiding causing or contributing to adverse human rights impacts and by addressing impacts directly linked to their operations, products, or services. This responsibility should also inform social media platforms when they respond to government requests that violate international human rights law, and in particular freedom of expression. We therefore urge X, Meta, and any other platform faced with such orders by the Turkish government to also follow these recommendations: Resist complying with arbitrary 8/A requests Refuse to comply with account blocking requests under Article 8/A of the Internet Law unless Turkish authorities identify the specific content at issue and provide sufficient reasoning and evidence demonstrating that the content gives rise to a clear, serious and imminent danger to the right to life and property, national security and public order, public health or other ground listed in the provision. Where account blocking orders provide sufficient information to enable a meaningful assessment, assess them against international human rights law and resist complying with blocking orders that restrict access to protected expression. This includes but is not limited to legally challenging such orders. Where relevant, limit restrictions in scope and duration, for example by restricting access only to the specific content identified in the order rather than withholding the entire account. Ensure transparency Immediately notify users when their accounts are withheld in Türkiye and provide them with the orders on which the restriction is based. This allows account holders to take necessary steps to challenge the orders. Provide transparency concerning account blocking measures, at least by publicly sharing the number of orders received, the number of orders complied with, and publishing case studies. This information is essential for enabling public scrutiny of government censorship and platforms’ role in it. Engage with Turkish civil society Meaningfully engage with Turkish civil society to understand the human rights implications and broader impact of platforms complying with account blocking measures, including the significance of the accounts targeted and the potential consequences of withholding them in Türkiye. Urgently review appeals to restrictions Review user appeals to account restrictions imposed in Türkiye in September and October 2026 and immediately restore access to accounts if the underlying orders fail to meet the requirements of identifying the specific content at issue, establishing a link between that content and the alleged threat to national security, public order and other grounds listed in Article 8/A, and providing adequate reasoning demonstrating that blocking the entire account is necessary and proportionate. We call on Turkish authorities to take urgent steps to end internet censorship and uphold freedom of expression, including by Immediately halting new restrictions on online content that violate freedom of expression, media freedom, and access to information as protected under international law and Türkiye’s human rights obligations.Restoring access to content which has been restricted in violation of international law and Türkiye’s freedom of expression obligations Signatories: ARTICLE 19 Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD)Human Rights WatchAmnesty International Association of European Journalists (AEJ)Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN)Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)Çağdaş Gazeteciler Derneği (ÇGD, Progressive Journalists Association)Foreign Media Association (FMA Turkey)IFEXInternational Press Institute (IPI)Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA)Norwegian Helsinki Committee (NHC)Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)P24 Platform for Independent JournalismPEN AmericaPEN DenmarkPEN InternationalPEN NorwaySouth East Europe Media Organisation (SEEMO)Turkey Litigation Support Project (TLSP)

items.title: Nigeria primed to be Africa’s industrial powerhouse— Ex-UNIDO DG
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole A former Director-General of the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO), Dr Kandeh Yumkella, has said Nigeria has the essential foundations to become Africa’s industrial powerhouse but must translate its huge market, natural resources and entrepreneurial capacity into competitive production and exports. Yumkella, who identified Nigeria’s financial depth and strategic position within the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as additional advantages, said the country’s industrial challenge was not a lack of ambition or enterprise, but the failure to convert its potential into measurable economic performance. He stated this in Lagos while delivering the 6th Adeola Odutola lecture with the theme, “Leveraging National Industrial Policy to Position Nigeria as Africa’s Industrial Hub”, organised by the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN). “Nigeria has the essential foundations for an industrial powerhouse. It has scale, resources, vibrant entrepreneurs, financial depth and strategic positioning to win equity in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). “Countries industrialise when policy translates into productive capacity, investment, technology, competitiveness and value addition to create jobs,” he said. Yumkella, however, noted that the country’s industrial performance remained below its potential, with manufacturing contributing about seven to eight per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), while manufactured exports generated only about three per cent of total export revenue. According to him, Nigeria’s exports of goods and services accounted for just 10.7 per cent of GDP, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen domestic production and expand access to international markets. “Nigeria’s 41 million micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) testify to the energy and resilience of the private sector. But potential is not performance,” he said. Yumkella identified unreliable electricity supply as a major obstacle to industrial competitiveness, noting that the national grid delivered about 5,000 to 6,000 megawatts against estimated demand exceeding 20,000 megawatts. He said manufacturers spent an estimated N1.34 trillion on self-generated electricity in 2025, compared with N781.68 billion in 2023, adding that energy accounted for between 35 and 40 per cent of production costs. He urged the government to harness the country’s abundant natural gas, hydropower and solar resources to provide reliable and affordable electricity for industries, while promoting regional energy markets across West Africa. The post Nigeria primed to be Africa’s industrial powerhouse— Ex-UNIDO DG appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tunisie | Faciliter la correction des dossiers Amen Social
items.description: Amen Social est le système tunisien de protection sociale destiné aux familles pauvres et à faible revenu, créé par la loi organique n° 2019-10 du 30 janvier 2019. Il prévoit des allocations mensuelles pour les ménages les plus nécessiteux, un accès à des soins de santé gratuits ou à tarif réduit via la Caisse nationale d’assurance maladie (Cnam) et une aide financière pour la rentrée scolaire et universitaire des enfants de familles bénéficiaires. Ce programme bénéficie à près de 10 % de la population tunisienne, constituant les ménages pauvres. Raison de plus pour qu'il soit réformé et adapté aux besoins de la population qui en a besoin. Gustavo Pessoa * Quand les revenus d’un ménage baissent, son dossier social doit pouvoir suivre. Une information devenue ancienne peut peser sur une décision d’aide, même lorsqu’elle était exacte au moment de son enregistrement. Pour une famille concernée, savoir comment la faire rectifier compte autant que la qualité du registre. La modernisation d’Amen Social doit rendre cette correction plus simple, plus compréhensible et suffisamment rapide pour rester utile. Le financement supplémentaire de 90 millions de dollars approuvé par la Banque mondiale le 27 mars 2026 offre l’occasion de renforcer cette exigence. L’opération soutient l’élargissement de la protection sociale et la modernisation de son administration, notamment le développement d’un registre intégré des bénéficiaires et l’extension des paiements numériques. Ce chantier devra permettre aux informations de mieux circuler tout en préservant la possibilité, pour chaque ménage, de faire rectifier celles qui le concernent. La Tunisie dispose déjà d’un cadre pour contester les décisions. Le ministère des Affaires sociales rappelle que le décret gouvernemental 2020-317 encadre l’accès à Amen Social et le règlement des griefs. Le registre du programme et son mécanisme de réclamation ne partent donc pas de zéro. La question est celle de leur efficacité pratique lorsque les données circulent davantage entre administrations et que le programme accueille de nouveaux bénéficiaires. A méliorer le dispositif et son suivi L’ évaluation publiée par la Banque mondiale en février 2026 décrit un dispositif de réclamation déjà opérationnel, associant le Bureau des relations avec le citoyen et les structures régionales. Plusieurs canaux permettent de déposer une plainte, dont les bureaux locaux, le courrier et le téléphone. Le projet prévoit aussi d’améliorer le dispositif et son suivi. Cette base doit guider la réforme, avec une attention particulière à ce qui se passe après le dépôt d’un recours. Pour le ménage, l’essentiel est de comprendre quelle information a influencé la décision et comment signaler un changement. Le motif communiqué devrait être assez précis pour permettre une démarche utile, sans exposer des données personnelles. Une explication générale sur l’inéligibilité risque de laisser le demandeur chercher la mauvaise pièce justificative ou retourner au mauvais guichet. Lorsqu’une information doit être vérifiée auprès d’un autre service, l’administration devrait organiser cet échange au lieu d’en faire supporter toute la charge à la famille. La possibilité de corriger une donnée mérite aussi d’être distinguée du désaccord avec les critères d’attribution. Une erreur sur un revenu, une situation familiale ou un document appelle une vérification factuelle. Une contestation de l’application des règles appelle une réponse motivée. Clarifier ces deux démarches faciliterait le travail des agents et éviterait de transformer chaque rectification en conflit sur l’ensemble du programme. Une correction justifiée peut conduire à réexaminer le dossier sans garantir automatiquement l’octroi d’une prestation. Les délais observés devraient devenir un indicateur public de la réforme. Dans le suivi déjà prévu, des résultats agrégés pourraient montrer le temps nécessaire pour recevoir une réponse, la proportion de dossiers encore en attente et les principaux motifs de rectification. Ces informations aideraient à repérer un blocage dans une région ou une procédure, sans publier l’identité des familles. Le nombre de plaintes reçues, pris isolément, serait insuffisant : un canal plus accessible peut faire augmenter les demandes tout en améliorant le service. Les voies physiques et téléphoniques restent importantes. Un changement de situation peut concerner une personne qui ne maîtrise pas les démarches en ligne, dispose d’une connexion irrégulière ou a besoin de l’aide d’un travailleur social. Le numérique devrait faciliter le traitement et le suivi de sa demande. Il devrait également permettre à l’agent qui l’accompagne de retrouver son dossier, pour éviter qu’elle raconte la même situation à chaque déplacement. Mieux orienter les ressources disponibles Cette attention aux recours relève aussi d’une bonne gestion financière. Une donnée corrigée aide à orienter les ressources vers les personnes qui répondent effectivement aux conditions du programme. Une décision compréhensible facilite le contrôle et réduit les démarches inutiles. À l’inverse, laisser une erreur se prolonger peut aggraver la difficulté que l’aide devait soulager et multiplier les coûts administratifs nécessaires pour la résoudre. Le nouveau financement doit donc soutenir une protection sociale capable d’apprendre de ses propres corrections. Les familles ont besoin d’un interlocuteur identifiable, d’une explication utilisable et d’une suite donnée à leur démarche. Rendre ces éléments visibles donnerait un sens concret à la modernisation : un dossier qui évolue avec la situation du ménage, et une administration qui sait reconnaître puis rectifier une information devenue fausse. * Professeur d’économie et de finance à la Fundação Getulio Vargas, au Brésil. items.title: Backward integration lifts manufacturing investment 102% to N1.33trn
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole Manufacturers’ drive to reduce dependence on imported inputs and foreign exchange (FX) has pushed investment in the sector up by 102.16 per cent to N1.33 trillion in 2025, from N658.81 billion in 2024, the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) has said. Director-General of MAN, Segun Ajayi-Kadir, disclosed this in the 2025 annual report of the association released recently, attributing the surge in investment to aggressive backward integration and expansion of local production capacity by manufacturers. According to him, the investment drive reflects efforts by manufacturers to reduce their exposure to foreign exchange illiquidity, while strengthening domestic supply chains and improving operational efficiency amid rising production and distribution costs. A half-yearly breakdown of the figures showed that manufacturing investment rose to N764.07 billion in the second half of 2025, from N567.82 billion in the first half, representing a 34.56 per cent increase. Ajayi-Kadir also highlighted manufacturers’ growing investment in distribution infrastructure, particularly the acquisition of their own vehicle fleets to manage rising energy costs and third-party haulage charges. With transportation and logistics expenses mounting, he said, manufacturers were increasingly investing in their own fleets to exercise greater control over distribution costs and protect their margins. To sustain the investment momentum and deepen local value addition, the MAN DG proposed a series of policy measures aimed at strengthening backward integration, expanding domestic sourcing and making government procurement more supportive of Nigerian industries. He advocated a tiered corporate tax rebate of between 10 and 15 per cent for companies that achieve certified local raw material sourcing thresholds of at least 40 per cent. He also proposed the establishment of a digital National Value Chain Portal to connect large-scale manufacturers with verified local small and medium-scale industrial (SMI) suppliers of raw materials and intermediate goods. On public procurement, Ajayi-Kadir called for the enactment of a Local Patronage Compliance Act requiring ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs) to give Nigerian manufacturers the right of first refusal in procurement. Under the proposal, a temporary Certificate of Non-Availability, issued by MAN through the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, would be required before government agencies could purchase products from foreign suppliers. He further recommended that budget releases to MDAs be tied to verifiable evidence of compliance with Executive Order 003 and the Federal Government’s Nigeria First Policy, including invoices showing purchases of Nigerian-made products. To ensure continuity and accountability, the MAN DG urged the National Assembly to pass the Nigeria Industrial Policy into law, making its targets and incentives legally binding and protecting them from arbitrary changes or abandonment by successive administrations. He also proposed a mandatory annual State of the Industrial Sector report to the National Assembly in the first quarter of every year to track implementation of the Nigeria Industrial Policy against measurable performance indicators. The proposals, he said, are aimed at translating rising investment into stronger domestic supply chains, greater local production capacity and sustainable industrial growth. items.title: BoG proposes new rules to ensure banks can always pay customers when they need their Money
items.description: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has proposed a new regulatory requirement that would compel banks to maintain sufficient high-quality liquid assets to cover their projected net cash outflows over a 30-day period of financial stress. The proposal is contained in the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) Directive, 2026 , an exposure draft published by the central bank on October 9, 2026, to solicit comments from the banking industry and the general public. In a notice on its website, the BoG said the consultation is being conducted in accordance with its Procedures for Issuance of Directives, 2020. Stakeholders have until November 30, 2026, to submit their comments. Under the proposed framework, banks would be required to maintain a Liquidity Coverage Ratio of at least 100 per cent. This means their stock of eligible, unencumbered high-quality liquid assets must be sufficient to cover their total net cash outflows projected over the next 30 calendar days under prescribed stress conditions. The measure is intended to strengthen banks’ ability to withstand sudden funding pressures and meet financial obligations during periods of significant market or institution-specific stress. According to the draft directive, the framework is designed to improve the banking sector’s capacity to absorb financial and economic shocks while reducing the risk that liquidity problems in individual banks spill over into the wider economy. How the proposed liquidity requirement would work The LCR would be calculated by dividing a bank’s stock of eligible high-quality liquid assets by its total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days. The qualifying assets must be capable of being converted into cash quickly, with little or no loss of value, and must be free from restrictions that would prevent their use during a period of stress. The directive identifies cash, qualifying balances held with the Bank of Ghana and eligible government securities among the assets that may qualify as high-quality liquid assets. Other eligible securities may also be included, subject to specified conditions and regulatory discounts, known as haircuts. The proposed framework places limits on the composition of the liquidity buffer. Level 2 assets would be capped at 40 per cent of the total stock of high-quality liquid assets, while Level 2B assets would be limited to 15 per cent. Banks would also be required to assess potential cash outflows arising from deposit withdrawals, reduced access to wholesale funding, maturing financing obligations and customers drawing on previously committed credit facilities. The draft further requires banks to conduct their own liquidity stress tests, including scenarios that are more severe and extend beyond the minimum 30-day supervisory requirement. Implementation timeline The BoG has proposed September 1, 2027, as the effective date of the directive. Banks would be required to align their internal policies, processes and systems with its provisions by August 31, 2027. The draft also provides for a one-year pilot period following publication, during which banks would submit quarterly reports to the central bank using prescribed templates. Monthly reporting would be required after the pilot period. The arrangements are intended to support the monitoring of banks’ liquidity positions and their compliance with the new regulatory framework. Consultation and stakeholder submissions The central bank is inviting banks and other interested stakeholders to examine the proposed requirements and submit comments before the directive is finalised. Submissions should be sent by email to bsdletters@bog.gov.gh no later than November 30, 2026. The BoG says it will consider all material comments received and provide written explanations addressing how they were treated in the final directive, including whether they were incorporated. The consultation offers banks and other stakeholders an opportunity to raise concerns about the proposed framework and recommend changes ahead of implementation. Part of broader banking-sector reforms The proposed LCR requirement forms part of the BoG’s broader regulatory framework for strengthening liquidity risk management in the banking sector. The exposure draft states that the directive is intended to complement the Liquidity Risk Management Directive, 2026, and the Liquidity Monitoring Tools Directive, 2026, providing both quantitative requirements and supporting liquidity-risk monitoring measures. While the LCR would establish a minimum benchmark for banks’ short-term liquidity buffers, its implementation could require adjustments to treasury operations, asset allocation, liquidity forecasting and regulatory reporting. The extent of these adjustments will depend on the final provisions adopted by the central bank following the consultation process. The proposal is therefore a significant development in the regulation of bank liquidity in Ghana, with the final requirements expected to shape how banks prepare for and respond to periods of financial stress.

items.title: Independence address, endless promises no specifics
items.description: By Dele Sobowale Bayo Onanuga, the Senior Special Adviser to the President, accused critics of writing their responses without reading Tinubu’s address. That is certainly not true about me. In fact, the address was read to me by Uncle Sam, the Publisher of Vanguard, in his house – while asking for my comments on a few statements. Unknown to Uncle Sam, at least until I told him, my team was out from 6am monitoring the situation with transport fares in several bus stations in Lagos State. By the time three of us reached Uncle Sam’s house, reports from thirteen popular bus stations were in. So, I can state authoritatively that the address was read from start to finish. And, it was underwhelming. Silence is better when a leader has nothing important to say. But, before commenting on the address, here is what we observed on October 1, 2026 at bus stops. Reports from most of the Northern states were most disappointing. Obviously, a state without any gas station cannot possibly crash transport fares. In search of gas fueled buses “CNG application” States fail to implement Tinubu’s low fare directive” – Report, October 2, 2026. Tinubu’s government has been characterized by talking first and thinking later since he announced “fuel subsidy is gone”. His Minister of Transport, if he has a competent one, should have told him the truth and saved him from self-embarrassment. Nigeria is not ready for the massive introduction of CNG which would reduce transport fares significantly. Now, he has another unfulfilled promise charged to his account. Apart from being on the road early on October 1, 2026, , three bus drivers operating on six major routes were recruited to report on the introduction of gas-fueled buses and the expected crash in transport fares arising from their introduction. President Tinubu promised Nigerians to crash transport fares on October 1. Nothing like that happened in most of Lagos. I was not surprised. Talking first, thinking later is FG policy. FG was unprepared for October 1, 2026 Permit me to recall what I wrote last week before October 1 about the promise made to crash transport fares nationwide. President Tinubu must have been deceived, once again, by his Ministers and advisers. Given the number of gas stations and vehicles available, even Lagos State could not have felt the impact. Promise of cheaper transport on October 1 “If you believe that, you will believe anything”. That is my usual response to any government promise made in panic and which cannot possibly be redeemed on time. Dreaming is not bad, as long as the dreamer(s) wake up to reality. Weekend Trust, September 26, 2026, exposed the false promise with its report titled “Nigeria’s Oct 1 Transport Deadline: Vision vs Reality”. Before that report, I have searched in vain for a new CNG station in Lagos Island and Mainland. The research was outsourced to friends living in Ikorodu, Epe, Magodo, Mushin, Ajegunle and Festac. The reports were uniformly depressing. But, I still kept hope alive. In the few places where CNG outlets were available, the queue and the cost of conversion to gas is discouraging potential customers. In Lagos, which has 15 gas stations, motorists in Eti-Osa, Epe, Agbowa, Lagos Island, Ikorodu, Yaba, Orile, Ajegunle etc would have to travel over 40 kilometres, one way, to buy gas for their cars. Then they will have to stay in the queue for hours as additional hardship. Obviously, most of Lagos State will not be ready for the announced cheaper fare promise on October 1. “No CNG facility in Taraba, Benue, Plateau” – Weekend Trust, September 26, 2026. It is difficult to imagine how Nigerians living in the three states will experience any relief on October 1 without a single gas station in sight. That is official propaganda at its worst. A little better are Rivers and Kogi States with three stations each. Less fortunate are: Gombe, Adamawa,Katsina, Ondo and Zamfara having one station for states which are twenty to fifty times the size of Lagos. There is no need to list all the states of the federation and the number of stations servicing each of them. The roll out is obviously too little, too late and will be followed by excuses after its failure. Predictably, the FG has remained silent on the failed promise to crash transport fares. Elsewhere in the world, heads would have rolled. Those who misled Tinubu and exposed him to ridicule would have been shown the way out. We wait to see what would follow another failed promise. Nothing said about insecurity “28 killed despite curfew in Plateau” – Daily Trust, October 5, 2026. “Mambilla’s descent into violence” – Daily Trust, Editorial, October 5, 2026. “Kidnappers slash ransom to N100m as outrage mounts” – PUNCH, October 5, 2026. As President Tinubu was speaking, urging Nigerians to glue their eyes to the dark tunnel in search of light, evil men were operating in every corner of Nigeria. On October 1, two buses conveying Youth Corpers to Abia and Akwa Ibom States were waylaid in Imo State in the South East. They were eventually rescued; but, not without lasting psychological traumas. The incident, now a recurring occurrence, now threatens the existence of the National Youth Service as never before. Early in the year, Tinubu vowed that the genocide in Jos would be the last on the Plateau. Several more have occurred since then. On October 4, 2026, gunmen proved the presidential promise worthless once again; 28 Fulanis reportedly paid the supreme price of living in a country where the government is failing in its primary duty. From the North Central the attention moved to the Northeast. The Daily Trust Editorial summarised for Nigerians the recurrent mayhem on the other Plateau – Mambilla. “Last week, a fresh clash between Mambilla residents and Fulani Pastoralists reportedly left at least seven people dead, 186 livestock killed and more than 340 homes burnt, forcing 1000 residents to flee their communities…”. Left unmentioned were acts of mindless violence committed elsewhere on October 1 alone. President Tinubu glossed over the leading cause of our slow development – insecurity. Only two explanations are possible. He is bereft of solutions; or he just hoped nobody would notice the omission. Yet, without security nationwide, rapid growth, which will actually light up the tunnel will remain a pipe dream. A few words on the address “Goals are dreams with deadlines” – Albert Einstein, 1879-1955. The address was replete with promises about the future but short on specific dates for accomplishment. There were significant achievements based on monetary policy and subsidy removal – exchange rate stability, tremendous rise in external reserves, vastly increased revenue collection and allocation, as well as 4.5 per cent GDP growth. But, these positive results have not reflected in improved social welfare for the masses of Nigeria. Virtually all the gains have accrued to the wealthy, the petroleum and financial sectors and telecommunication networks. Manufacturers are hanging on the ropes. Right now only the President, his appointees and party members can see the light at the end of the tunnel – when 4000MW guaranteed per day is still a mirage. items.title: Sahara occidental : l’Espagne peut-elle céder le contrôle de l’espace aérien au Maroc ?
items.description: L’Espagne peut-elle transférer au Maroc la gestion de l’espace aérien du Sahara occidental sans préjuger du statut international du territoire ? La question dépasse les considérations techniques liées à la sécurité aérienne. Le Sahara occidental demeure inscrit sur la liste des territoires non autonomes des Nations unies. Le Maroc n’y figure pas comme puissance administrante. Le processus de décolonisation reste inachevé et le droit du peuple sahraoui à l’autodétermination demeure au cœur du dossier. Le Maroc est la puissance occupante et l’Espagne reste la puissance administrante de jure quels que soient les propos tenus par les officiels espagnols. l'Espagne ne peut pas se défaire unilatéralement de ses responsabilités. Et elle restera la puissance administrante tant qu'il n'y aura pas de solution définitive. l'avis juridique de Hans Correl, conseiller juridique de l'ONU de 2002 precise que le honteux accord de Madrid n'a transféré au Maroc ni la souveraineté ni le statut de puissance administrante. Dans ces conditions, un transfert de la gestion de l’espace aérien au Maroc soulèverait une question politique et juridique majeure. Une délégation technique ne vaut pas reconnaissance de souveraineté. Toutefois, confier à Rabat la gestion aérienne d’un territoire dont le statut définitif reste en suspens risquerait de consolider sa position de fait, sans règlement préalable de la question de décolonisation. Espace aérien du Sahara occidental : que va faire l’Espagne ? L’Espagne, ancienne puissance administrante du Sahara occidental, conserve donc une responsabilité politique et morale particulière. Elle devrait éviter tout transfert susceptible de préjuger du statut du territoire, tant qu’une solution conforme au droit international et au droit à l’autodétermination du peuple sahraoui n’aura pas été trouvée. La sécurité aérienne relève des normes de l’Organisation de l’aviation civile internationale. Elle ne saurait servir de fondement à une reconnaissance implicite de souveraineté. Dans ce contexte, la démarche du Parti populaire espagnol mérite d’être soulignée. Le PP demande au gouvernement de Pedro Sánchez de maintenir la gestion de l’espace aérien sous contrôle espagnol, de garantir le respect des exigences de l’OACI et d’informer les institutions canariennes des négociations avec Rabat. Il réclame également un débat parlementaire et l’intervention des organismes internationaux compétents avant toute décision. Cette initiative renforce la nécessité de dissocier la coopération aéronautique du règlement du statut international du Sahara occidental. L’Espagne ne doit pas offrir au Maroc un cadeau politique au détriment de la juste cause du peuple sahraoui et de son droit inaliénable à l’autodétermination. L’article Sahara occidental : l’Espagne peut-elle céder le contrôle de l’espace aérien au Maroc ? est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: ‘‘La Mission’’ de Mohamed Benchicou | Derrière Tiguentourine, les questions qui dérangent
items.description: Il faut relire ‘‘La Mission’’ (Koukou Éditions, Algérie, 2014). Pas comme un thriller. Comme un document politique déguisé en roman. Publié en 2014 chez Koukou Éditions, le livre de Mohamed Benchicou revient sur l’attaque du complexe gazier de Tiguentourine, au sud-est de l’Algérie, non loin de la frontière libyenne, en janvier 2013, pour explorer ce que l’événement pourrait dissimuler : intérêts énergétiques, rivalités au sommet de l’État et stratégies étrangères. Djamal Guettala L’auteur ne se limite pas au récit de la prise d’otages. Il bâtit une intrigue autour d’une question autrement sensible : les intérêts économiques et les luttes de pouvoir ont-ils pu peser sur le destin de ce site stratégique ? La question nourrit le roman ; elle ne constitue pas, à elle seule, une preuve. Le 16 janvier 2013, un groupe armé attaque le complexe gazier de Tiguentourine, près d’In Amenas. Des centaines de personnes sont prises en otage. L’intervention des forces algériennes met fin à la crise, au prix de lourdes pertes humaines. L’attaque marque durablement l’industrie gazière algérienne et les relations du pays avec ses partenaires étrangers. Un an plus tard, Benchicou choisit de déplacer le regard. Dans ‘‘La Mission’’ , Tiguentourine n’est pas seulement le théâtre d’une opération terroriste : le site devient le point de rencontre d’intérêts industriels, de convoitises financières et de rivalités politiques. La dimension romanesque lui permet de relier des éléments qui, dans le débat public, restent souvent séparés. L’auteur donne lui-même la clé de son approche : «Je n’ai été amené à connaître Tatiana que parce que l’attaque de Tiguentourine est une affaire de fric, de luttes d’influence, de rivalités de pouvoirs…» Cette phrase annonce le parti pris du livre. Les faits historiques sont établis : l’attaque, la prise d’otages et l’intervention militaire. Les connexions politiques et économiques mises en scène par Benchicou relèvent, elles, de sa construction romanesque. Cette frontière doit rester claire, sans pour autant réduire le livre à un simple exercice de fiction. Les intérêts gaziers et les rivalités du pouvoir Dans le récit, British Petroleum occupe une place centrale. L’entreprise britannique exploite le site avec ses partenaires. Benchicou imagine qu’après la catastrophe de Deepwater Horizon, BP cherche à céder ses actifs algériens et à revoir le modèle de sécurité de ses installations. La question de la propriété et de la protection du complexe devient alors un ressort majeur de l’intrigue. Mikhail Fridman, homme d’affaires russe né à Lviv, apparaît sous les traits de Tatiana-Johanna dans les ramifications du récit. Intéressé par le rachat du site, il incarne les convoitises financières qui entourent cette infrastructure stratégique. Sir William Thompson, envoyé en mission par Downing Street, est chargé d’examiner la situation. À travers lui, Benchicou introduit la dimension britannique et les calculs diplomatiques liés aux intérêts énergétiques. Ces éléments donnent sa cohérence à l’intrigue, mais ne démontrent pas qu’une opération de cession, les manœuvres étrangères et l’attaque terroriste auraient été coordonnées dans la réalité. Le roman construit un scénario politique ; il ne livre pas une démonstration judiciaire. L’analyse s’étend ensuite aux rapports de force algériens. Mohamed Mediène, dit Toufik, et le DRS occupent une place importante dans la représentation d’un pouvoir traversé par les rivalités. Benchicou suggère que l’attaque pourrait s’inscrire dans une recomposition des équilibres sécuritaires et politiques. Cette lecture doit être attribuée à l’auteur : aucune conclusion judiciaire ne permet d’établir que Toufik ou des acteurs étrangers auraient organisé ou facilité l’attaque. L’arrière-plan est celui de l’Algérie de 2013-2014, au moment où se prépare le quatrième mandat d’Abdelaziz Bouteflika. Benchicou rapproche intérêts pétroliers, puissances étrangères et continuité du régime dans une formule accusatrice : «la connivence entre des capitales occidentales, la pègre pétrolière internationale et l’autocratie archaïque locale qui ambitionnait de se reconduire pour un quatrième mandat». Cette formule résume sa charge politique. Elle exprime une interprétation romanesque des rapports entre argent, pouvoir et intérêts étrangers, non une conclusion établie sur les responsabilités dans le drame de Tiguentourine. Le livre a été accueilli favorablement, mais sa portée politique semble être restée au second plan. Or, au-delà de l’intrigue, son intérêt réside aussi dans les questions qu’il soulève sur la vulnérabilité des infrastructures stratégiques et sur les rapports entre souveraineté nationale et intérêts économiques. Presse | Mohamed Benchicou inhumé finalement à Alger Un livre qui résiste au temps Depuis la parution de ‘‘La Mission’’ , le paysage politique algérien a changé. Bouteflika a obtenu son quatrième mandat, avant de quitter le pouvoir. Mohamed Mediène a été écarté de la tête du DRS, ensuite réorganisé puis dissous. Ces événements éclairent le contexte dans lequel Benchicou écrivait ; ils ne confirment pas rétrospectivement ses hypothèses sur Tiguentourine. La portée du livre tient ailleurs : dans sa volonté de dépasser le récit immédiat d’un attentat pour interroger les intérêts et les rapports de force qui entourent les lieux stratégiques. On peut discuter ses hypothèses, contester ses rapprochements et rappeler les limites de sa démonstration. On ne peut ignorer la question qui traverse son récit : derrière les événements, quels intérêts se croisent et quelles vérités restent à établir ? Mohamed Benchicou est mort le 24 septembre 2026. Avec ‘‘La Mission’’ , il laisse un texte qui témoigne de sa manière d’interroger le pouvoir et de mettre en cause les récits trop vite refermés. Relire ce livre ne revient pas à transformer ses hypothèses en certitudes, mais à reprendre les questions qu’il a posées. Cette mission n’est pas terminée. L’article ‘‘La Mission’’ de Mohamed Benchicou | Derrière Tiguentourine, les questions qui dérangent est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: APC polls show Tinubu will win 2027 election — Yilwatda
items.description: The National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Nentawe Yilwatda, says the party’s internal polls indicate that President Bola Tinubu will win the 2027 presidential election. Yilwatda disclosed this during an appearance on Channels Television’s Sunday Politics , where he said the party had conducted surveys across states and obtained statistics showing Tinubu ahead of his potential challengers. “We have done fact-finding; we are leading. We have done our polls. We have our own polls that give us the real statistics across the states,” he said. Asked whether the polls indicated that Tinubu would win the election, Yilwatda responded, “Of course!” The APC chairman said the ruling party was not intimidated by opposition parties, including the African Democratic Congress (ADC), associated with former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), associated with Peter Obi. He argued that the opposition parties’ inability to win elections ahead of 2027 gave the APC an advantage. Yilwatda also compared Tinubu with Atiku, describing the incumbent president as “far better” than the former vice-president. Defending the administration’s economic policies, he said its tax reforms had expanded the tax net and increased government revenue, while benefiting the poorest Nigerians. He also cited changes in the power sector, saying state governments had been empowered to generate, transmit and distribute electricity. Yilwatda acknowledged the hardship associated with rising petrol prices but maintained that the situation was temporary. “What we are passing through in Nigeria, for example, at this moment, is temporary. The increase in the cost of fuel is temporary. Nigerians believe in us,” he said. On allegations that the APC protects its members from prosecution, Yilwatda said some party members were facing court proceedings and insisted that no one was shielded from the law. He added that the party was reviewing its presidential campaign council list and would inaugurate it soon. Yilwatda also said he had no objection to individuals or groups, including the Rainbow Coalition associated with FCT Minister Nyesom Wike, supporting Tinubu’s re-election bid. He dismissed the “Tinubu Must Go” campaign as an opposition-driven effort that did not reflect Nigerians’ views of the president. The post APC polls show Tinubu will win 2027 election — Yilwatda appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Atiku demands names of firms printing INEC’s ballot papers
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar has challenged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to disclose who is printing sensitive materials for the 2027 elections, warning that opaque contracts and key departmental redeployments could undermine confidence in the polls. His central concern is that Nigerians could head into a decisive election without knowing who is producing their ballots, how the contracts were awarded or what safeguards exist against political interference. In a statement by his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, for the African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku demanded explanations for reported changes in INEC’s Electoral Operations Department and allegations that a substantial share of sensitive election materials had been allocated to private contractors. Reports indicate that Director Isa Magaji Gum was moved from Electoral Operations to the Voter Registry Department, while Mrs Oluyemi Titilayo Adeyemi-Showunmi was appointed to head Electoral Operations. Dr Lawrence Bayode was also identified as head of Information and Communication Technology. “These departments are at the heart of election administration. INEC must explain these decisions, publish the criteria applied and show that every appointment and redeployment followed due process, was based on merit and was free from political interference.” Atiku also demanded that INEC confirm or deny whether Hitech, or any company associated with it, had secured a contract to print sensitive election materials. He alleged that more than half of the materials, including presidential ballot assets, might have been allocated to an undisclosed company believed to be based in France. He further questioned reports that the Nigerian Security Printing and Minting Plc was printing materials for only 15 to 17 states, leaving private firms to handle the remainder. “Nigerians should not have to depend on unnamed sources to discover who is producing their ballots,” he said, demanding the disclosure of contractors, allocations, procurement methods and security arrangements. Atiku argued that any contract awarded to Hitech or an associated company would raise questions about INEC’s neutrality, citing publicly reported business ties between the Chagoury family, which owns Hitech, and the Tinubu family. The former vice-president also pointed to controversy surrounding Hitech contracts under President Bola Tinubu’s administration, including the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway project. “If neither Hitech nor a company associated with it has been selected, INEC must say so clearly and put the matter beyond doubt,” he said. He urged the Central Bank of Nigeria to disclose its banknote-printing allocations and explain the roles of domestic and foreign contractors, while calling on INEC to maximise domestic security-printing capacity and ensure every ballot and result sheet is protected by a transparent chain of custody. Atiku warned that Nigerians battered by economic hardship would resist any attempt to subvert their votes, insisting that the 2027 election must not become an instrument for prolonging the Tinubu administration’s hold on power. “Let there be no mistake: Nigerians will not accept a stolen election. Any attempt to rig the 2027 polls will be met with determined resistance through the ballot, lawful civic action, and every other democratic channel available to the people.” He said the ADC would monitor INEC’s preparations and alert domestic and international observers to any lack of transparency, insisting that the commission must prove its impartiality through verifiable disclosures. items.title: Hotline Documentary: ‘Silent Football’ to air on JoyPrime and JoyNews today
items.description: A new Hotline/JoySports documentary, Silent Football: When Passion Speaks Without Words, will air on JoyPrime and JoyNews on Monday, October 12, 2026, which will explore the achievements of Ghana’s deaf footballers and the challenges they face in pursuit of their dreams. Produced by Haruna Mubarak, the documentary takes viewers into the world of deaf football in the country, following players from their respective clubs to the national team, the Black Wonders. Through the experiences of players and football administrators, the production explores how the team trains, communicates and competes, relying on visual awareness, gestures and instinct to navigate a game often dominated by sound. Beyond the action on the pitch, Silent Football examines the difficulties facing the Black Wonders, especially concerns about the support available to players who have represented Ghana in international competitions. Despite their achievements at continental and regional levels, the team continues to face challenges in securing the resources and institutional backing needed to compete on the international stage. The documentary also features the team’s patroness and current Minister of Environment, Science and Technology of Ghana, Zanetor Rawlings, who speaks about the quality of the players and the lack of support confronting the team. Silent Football: When Passion Speaks Without Words will air on JoyPrime at 8:30 am and JoyNews at 8:30 pm on Monday, October 12, 2026.

items.title: NDPC examines how evidence shapes Ghana’s development planning and policy decisions
items.description: The National Development Planning Commission (NDPC) is reviewing how research and other forms of evidence are generated, accessed and used to guide national development planning and policy decisions in Ghana. The Commission has reviewed preliminary findings from a study led by Mettalytics, with the Ghana case study conducted by a team from the University of Cape Coast (UCC). The findings point to challenges in ensuring that available evidence is effectively integrated into the planning process and influences policy decisions. Presenting the findings, Prof. William Cantah of UCC said the main challenge was not necessarily the availability of evidence, but how it moved through the planning process and informed decisions. He identified institutional arrangements, political priorities, timing, access to decision-makers, relationships, ownership and technical capacity as key factors influencing evidence use. Discussions with NDPC directors and senior officials examined the study’s scope, the sectors and stakeholders covered, and the relationship between political priorities and technical evidence in shaping development policies. The Director-General of the NDPC, Dr Audrey Smock Amoah, welcomed the presentation and said the Commission would review the full report and provide comments and feedback. She also stressed the importance of clearly defining the study’s scope to ensure its findings are properly understood and applied to Ghana’s national development planning process.

items.title: Education Ministry calls urgent talks to break GAUA strike deadlock
items.description: The Education Ministry has called an urgent meeting with the leadership of the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) and the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) to resolve the ongoing strike and restore normal operations at affected tertiary institutions. The meeting, scheduled for Monday, October 12, 2026, is intended to create room for constructive dialogue towards an amicable resolution of the impasse. In a statement signed by its Press Secretary, Hashmin Mohammed, the Ministry urged all parties to approach the talks in good faith, mindful of the impact of the industrial action on students, university communities and the broader national interest. “Government urges the leadership of GAUA to seize this opportunity for meaningful engagement and work collaboratively with the relevant stakeholders towards an early resolution of the impasse,” the statement said. The Ministry reaffirmed the government’s commitment to addressing the concerns of organised labour through established negotiation mechanisms and constructive engagement. It expressed hope that the meeting would produce a positive outcome and pave the way for a swift return to normal academic and administrative activities across affected institutions. The statement did not detail the grievances behind the strike or outline specific proposals for resolving them.

items.title: Another slain seaman’s family seeks return of his remains
items.description: KARACHI: Just days after kidnapped sailors from MT Honour 25 were reunited with their families, another Pakistani seafarer’s family is seeking the return of his mortal remains, following his demise after his ship came under attack near the Strait of Hormuz last month. Muhammad Hammad Obaida, a third engineer and crew member aboard the Panama-flagged oil tanker MT El Gaia, was killed in an attack on the vessel on Sept 13, off the coast of Oman. Nearly a month on, however, the grieving family in Pakistan, including his three-year-old son and pregnant wife, is still waiting for his repatriation. Media reports provide conflicting accounts of the incident, which took place north of Oman’s Musandam peninsula. According to multiple accounts, the tanker came under attack on Sept 13, while Reuters reported that it was towed to an Omani port around five days later. Pregnant widow, toddler await Hammad Obaida’s body after he perished in attack off Oman coast last month While US and Iranian authorities traded blame over who was behind the strike, the bodies of two sailors — a Pakistani and an Indian — who had perished in an engine room fire were only discovered days after the incident, when the men were found to be missing during a headcount. According to Hammad’s family, they came to know about the incident through one of his colleagues on Sept 26. Hammad had left home only a few days earlier, on Sept 6. Just a day before the attack, he had spoken to his mother over a video call. “He was showing me around the ship… He was happy to be back at work,” his mother, Ather Pervaiz, told Dawn. Hammad, 34, was a qualified marine engineer who had graduated from Glasgow University in the UK. When his younger brother Fawwad took out his phone to show us a picture, Hammad’s three-year-old son, Musa, who had been busy playing with blocks on the floor, suddenly looked up and ran to take the phone from his uncle. “This is my Baba,” the toddler exclaimed, adding, “He is with Allah Mian [God Almighty] now.” He kissed the phone screen as both his elders struggled to hold back tears. “Hammad’s son needs to say a final goodbye to him. His young widow is expecting their second child. His father, brother, sisters and I have accepted what happened as God’s will. But please bring us his remains so that we can at least give him a respectful burial,” Ms Pervaiz said quietly. Fawwad explained that despite writing countless letters and rea­ching out to the Pakistan Embassy in Oman, the Foreign Office and the prime minister through social media, the family had received no clear official response. “We also approached the Sindh government… and were told that the matter was in the government’s knowledge,” he added. DNA sample Fawwad said the Pakistani embassy in Oman had confirmed that two bodies were awaiting DNA testing in the country, but no Pakistani authority had collected a DNA sample from the family to expedite identification. “I am also in touch with Vivek, the brother of Indian seafarer Sumit Kumar, whose body was found alongside my brother’s,” he stated. When contacted, the Foreign Office confirmed that the bodies of a Pakistani and an Indian seafarer were lying in a hospital mortuary in Oman, awaiting DNA testing for identification. Responding to Dawn’s query, the FO spokesperson said the bodies had been severely disfigured, making DNA testing necessary and delaying the repatriation of the remains to their families. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

items.title: NCCE engages women in North East Gonja on rule of law, anti-corruption
items.description: The North East Gonja District Directorate of the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE), has engaged women’s groups on the need to promote the rule of law, resist corruption and demand accountability in their communities. The engagement, held at Fuu with support from the German Development Cooperation, was a follow-up campaign aimed at consolidating the gains made during an earlier engagement and empowering women to become active champions of transparency, accountability and the rule of law. A total of 52 women drawn from various identifiable groups including hairdressers, dressmakers and market women participated in the engagement. Madam Martha Bagbin, the North East Gonja District Director, NCCE, urged the participants to raise up against corruption and become agents of positive change in their communities. Mr Sulemana Fuseini, an Officer of School for Life in the district, who was a resource person, interacted with the participants to assess the impact of the earlier engagement and ascertain how they had applied the knowledge acquired. Some participants shared experiences of how the previous engagement had empowered them to ask questions and demand clarification on activities they suspected to be corrupt. They cited instances where they were asked to make certain payments during antenatal and postnatal services and said that after seeking clarification and questioning the payments, some of the monies were refunded to them. They also demonstrated increased awareness of corrupt practices including giving money or other items to people in positions of authority to access services. Mr Fuseini encouraged them to apply the principles of the rule of law, resist corrupt practices and demand accountability from duty-bearers. He urged them to promote ethical practices within their communities and use the knowledge gained to influence others to uphold integrity and transparency. The participants were also educated on existing legal protection and mechanisms for reporting corruption and encouraged to serve as peer educators and advocates for integrity, accountability and the rule of law within their associations and communities.

items.title: NDPC reviews 2004 planning guidelines to reflect changes in decentralised system
items.description: The National Development Planning Commission (NDPC) has begun a nationwide review of guidelines governing Regional Planning Coordinating Units (RPCUs) and District Planning Coordinating Units (DPCUs) to improve development planning, coordination and reporting across Ghana’s decentralised governance system. The exercise, supported by GIZ’s PAIRed programme, is intended to update the existing guidelines, which were developed in 2004, to reflect changes in institutional arrangements, planning and budgeting processes, monitoring requirements and the growing use of digital systems in public administration. The nationwide consultations began on October 5, 2026, with engagements in the Upper East and Central Regions. The Greater Accra session, held on October 6, brought together stakeholders to assess the existing guidelines, identify implementation challenges and recommend practical improvements based on their experiences. Welcoming participants, the Chief Director of the Greater Accra Regional Coordinating Council, Rev. Harry Nii Kwatei Owoo, said the current guidelines no longer adequately reflected the environment in which RPCUs and DPCUs operate. He urged participants to identify gaps and propose measures that would make the revised document more relevant and effective. The Director-General of the NDPC, Dr Audrey Smock Amoah, said the review must be grounded in the experiences of officials directly involved in development planning and coordination at the regional and district levels. She noted that the process offered an opportunity to align the guidelines with current institutional arrangements, planning requirements and technological developments. Dr Amoah also stressed the need for regional and district authorities to prepare and submit development plans and annual progress reports on time, warning that delays could affect national development planning, monitoring and reporting. She thanked the Greater Accra Regional Coordinating Council, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies, GIZ and other stakeholders for supporting the exercise, and urged participants to make practical recommendations to strengthen coordination across the decentralised planning system. The consultations will continue across the country, with stakeholder feedback expected to inform the finalisation of the revised RPCU and DPCU guidelines. The PAIRed programme is commissioned by Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, co-financed by the European Union in Ghana and the Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, and implemented by GIZ in partnership with Ghana’s Ministry of Finance.

items.title: Trade Ministry commends Prisons Service for using art to drive inmate rehabilitation
items.description: The Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry has commended the Ghana Prisons Service for using creative arts to promote inmate rehabilitation, skills development and economic empowerment. Speaking on behalf of the Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, Deputy Minister Sampson Ahi said art could serve as a powerful tool for human transformation, mutual understanding and the recognition of shared humanity. He made the remarks as the special guest of honour at the maiden Director-General and Adehyee’s Art Exhibition, where he stressed that correctional work must go beyond confinement to equip inmates with practical skills, rebuild their self-confidence and prepare them for economic opportunities and successful reintegration into society. Mr Ahi also highlighted the potential of Ghana’s creative arts sector to generate employment, promote entrepreneurship and contribute to national development. He called for exhibitions of this nature to become sustainable platforms for talent discovery, public-private partnerships and the commercialisation of artworks produced by inmates. He further urged the public to look beyond the past mistakes of incarcerated persons, abandon stigmatisation and recognise their dignity and potential to contribute meaningfully to society. The Director-General of the Ghana Prisons Service, Mrs Patience Baffoe-Bonnie, said the initiative formed part of the Service’s broader Think Prisons 360 Degrees philosophy, which seeks to transform the institution from a purely custodial facility into a self-sustaining, development-oriented correctional system.

Books, brushes and second chances: Dr Abena Asomaning launches three titles to support prison outreach
items.description: Author, advocate and artist Dr Abena Nyarkoa Asomaning has launched three books and auctioned her original paintings to support incarcerated women, young people and former inmates rebuilding their lives. The event, dubbed “In Full Bloom: Art, Words & Legacy,” took place at the Mövenpick Ambassador Hotel in Accra, bringing together diplomats, representatives of the Bank of Ghana, business leaders, development partners and supporters of the Angel-Zoe Foundation. The three books— Women’s Leadership in Africa , The Shrewd You and Bloom —were unveiled during the evening. Proceeds from the painting auction will support the Foundation’s work. The event was chaired by His Royal Majesty Drolor Bosso Adamtey I, Se Mantse, Paramount King of the Shai Traditional Area, and moderated by broadcaster Frema Adunyame. In his remarks, Drolor Bosso Adamtey I praised Dr Asomaning’s commitment to using her knowledge, experience and creativity to serve others. “A book represents more than pages and ink. It represents the ideas, experiences and convictions of the person who wrote it,” he said. He described the launch of three books as a significant achievement, made more meaningful by her work beyond writing. “Her work with incarcerated people, particularly women, and her commitment to helping people reintegrate into society remind us that leadership is also about service,” he said. “Today, we are therefore celebrating not only three books and a collection of paintings, but a body of work that seeks to give people another opportunity.” Reflecting on Women’s Leadership in Africa , he welcomed men’s support for efforts to advance women’s leadership, noting that families, institutions and communities benefit when women can contribute fully. Delivering the keynote address, the Director-General of the Ghana Prisons Service, Mrs Patience Baffoe-Bonnie, described creativity and culture as important pillars of national development. She encouraged guests to support people who use their talents to serve society and stressed the importance of helping former prisoners reintegrate with dignity. “Please buy books. Kindly read them and share them,” she urged. Dr Erika Mamley Osae, who reviewed Women’s Leadership in Africa , described it as an examination of African leadership through women’s experiences. “Leadership, like the elephant, looks different depending on where you are standing,” she said. She noted that the book places historical queens and warriors alongside contemporary women leading in politics, business and their communities. Naa Ayeleysa Quaynor-Mettle read excerpts from all three books. Guests also watched two short films: Beyond the Pages , which explored the Angel-Zoe Foundation’s story, and The Artist Within , which focused on Dr Asomaning’s work as a painter. Her daughter introduced her to the audience. For Dr Asomaning, the occasion offered an opportunity to reflect on nearly two decades of work with the prison service. She said her research among juvenile offenders revealed concerns about prolonged detention and inadequate legal support for children. She subsequently established the Justice Civic Dialogues with the Judicial Training Institute to create a platform for justice institutions to discuss these challenges. Her service on a prison discharge board also deepened her understanding of the difficulties people face after leaving prison. “Freedom does not always feel like relief. Sometimes it is a rite of repair,” she said. Through the Angel-Zoe Foundation, her work includes providing food, healthcare, skills training, counselling and employment support to people leaving prison. The Foundation also helps former inmates rebuild relationships with families who may have rejected them. Its programmes include monthly masterclasses for young women and workshops for prison officers on issues such as United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325. “There is so much goodness in there if you give them an opportunity,” Dr Asomaning said. “Some of them didn’t have to be in prison at all.” She recalled former inmates who had gone on to teach at universities and serve in the military abroad, experiences that strengthened her belief in giving people opportunities beyond incarceration. Dr Asomaning thanked those who had supported her work over the years, including the men who had encouraged her efforts and the French government, which supported her doctoral studies in France. As she enters her 20th year with the prison service, she has appealed for continued support for young people and incarcerated women. She also thanked guests who purchased books and paintings to support the initiative. “May these books reach many readers,” Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie said in her closing remarks. The three books are available on Amazon.

items.title: Treasury bill auction oversubscribed by 53.5% as yields fall across maturities
items.description: Government has raised approximately GH¢4.41 billion in its latest Treasury bill auction, exceeding its GH¢2.87 billion target by about 53.5% as investor demand remained strong and yields declined across all three maturities. The auction results show that investors tendered bids across the 91-day, 182-day and 364-day instruments, with the Treasury accepting more than its target despite offering lower returns than in the previous auction. The 91-day bill attracted GH¢3.29 billion in bids, of which GH¢3.01 billion was accepted. The 182-day instrument received GH¢1.31 billion in tenders, with GH¢1.26 billion accepted, while the 364-day bill attracted GH¢468 million in bids, of which GH¢136 million was taken up. The acceptance pattern indicates that the Treasury relied mainly on the shorter-dated instruments to meet its financing needs, accepting less than a third of the bids submitted for the one-year bill. Yields declined across all three maturities. The rate on the 91-day bill fell to 4.60% from 4.64%, while the 182-day yield eased to 6.28% from 6.32%. The 364-day rate also dropped to 9.75% from 9.80%. Although the reductions were modest, the lower rates suggest investors were willing to accept slightly reduced returns on government securities. The difference between the 91-day and 364-day yields remained significant, with the longer-dated instrument offering a higher return in exchange for a longer commitment of funds. The strong uptake could support government’s efforts to manage short-term borrowing costs if demand persists in subsequent auctions. However, future results will be important in determining whether yields continue to decline and how much flexibility the Treasury has to reduce its financing costs.
