items.title: Burkina Faso : Charles Kaboré lance la Ligue de l’espoir pour les jeunes footballeurs
items.description: L’Ambassadeur pour le sport burkinabè, Charles Kaboré, a procédé, le 10 octobre 2026, au lancement de la première édition de la Ligue de l’espoir (LIDE), au stade Wobi de Bobo-Dioulasso. Cette compétition entend offrir davantage de temps de jeu aux jeunes footballeurs âgés de 13 à 17 ans durant l’année scolaire. Le football des jeunes se dote d’un nouveau cadre de compétition au Burkina Faso. Lancée au stade Wobi de Bobo-Dioulasso, la Ligue de l’espoir (LIDE) ambitionne de contribuer à l’encadrement des jeunes talents et à leur progression sportive grâce à des matchs organisés tout au long de l’année scolaire. Pour la saison 2026-2027, la compétition regroupe 16 équipes réparties en deux poules de huit formations, issues de Bobo-Dioulasso et de Ouagadougou. Elle cible les joueurs âgés de 13 à 17 ans, avec pour objectif de leur permettre de multiplier les rencontres et de développer leurs aptitudes dans un cadre compétitif. Pour Charles Kaboré, initiateur de la compétition, cette première édition constitue une étape importante dans la valorisation des talents burkinabè. « C’est une grande satisfaction. Comme on le dit, c’est important de valoriser nos talents. Grâce à la vision du Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, on voit loin. Cette compétition est mise en place pour que les jeunes puissent s’exprimer tout au long de l’année scolaire (…) C’est une phase pilote en se disant que ça va s’étendre sur toute l’étendue du territoire. On voit à court, moyen et long terme », a-t-il laissé entendre. « Cette compétition offre le cadre pour que les jeunes s’expriment », Ousmane Ouattara À travers cette initiative, la LIDE entend offrir aux jeunes footballeurs des occasions supplémentaires de pratiquer leur discipline et de se confronter aux exigences de la compétition. À cet âge, la régularité des matchs et la qualité de l’encadrement jouent un rôle important dans le développement des capacités techniques et tactiques des joueurs. Présent à la cérémonie de lancement, le ministre secrétaire général du gouvernement, Ousmane Ouattara, a également salué une initiative qui place la jeunesse au cœur du développement du sport. Selon lui, la Ligue de l’espoir s’inscrit dans la dynamique des actions entreprises pour traduire cette vision en réalisations concrètes. « La Ligue de l’espoir s’inscrit dans cette vision. Cette compétition offre le cadre pour que les jeunes s’expriment, mais aussi leur donner l’opportunité d’être détectés par des grands clubs. C’est l’occasion alors pour nous de saluer le promoteur et de lui apporter la caution et le soutien des plus hautes autorités » , a-t-il déclaré. Au-delà du temps de jeu, la compétition pourrait ainsi constituer une vitrine pour les jeunes joueurs en quête de visibilité. Les rencontres permettront aux participants de se mesurer à d’autres équipes et de faire valoir leur potentiel devant les acteurs du football. Rahimo FC remporte le match inaugural Le lancement de la Ligue de l’espoir a été marqué par une confrontation entre Rahimo FC et Vitesse FC, deux formations de la zone de Bobo-Dioulasso. Au terme d’une rencontre disputée, les jeunes joueurs de Rahimo FC se sont imposés sur le score de 3 buts à 2. Cette victoire permet à Rahimo FC de réussir son entrée dans la compétition, tandis que Vitesse FC devra se remobiliser pour la suite du championnat. Avec cette première édition, la Ligue de l’espoir pose les bases d’un dispositif destiné à accompagner la progression des jeunes footballeurs burkinabè. Présentée comme une phase pilote, l’initiative ambitionne de s’étendre progressivement à l’ensemble du territoire national. items.title: Musique : Joodal dévoile « Baas-Néré », un premier album sous le signe de l’accomplissement
items.description: L’artiste chanteur burkinabè Joël Agom Ouedé, connu sous le nom de scène Joodal, a présenté son tout premier album, « Baas-Néré », le 9 octobre 2026. Composé de onze titres, ce disque marque une nouvelle étape dans la carrière du musicien, après près de dix ans de singles, d’un maxi et de collaborations entre le Burkina Faso, le Ghana et le Nigeria. Après plusieurs années de travail et d’expérimentation musicale, Joodal franchit un nouveau cap avec la sortie de son premier album. Intitulé « Baas-Néré », qui signifie « bon accomplissement » en mooré, ce projet traduit la vision d’un artiste pour qui le chemin parcouru ne prend tout son sens qu’avec l’aboutissement. Originaire du Nahouri, Joël Agom Ouedé grandit dans un environnement musical. Fils d’une chanteuse, il rejoint la chorale de sa mère à l’âge de 12 ans et y passe six années. Cette expérience contribue à façonner sa voix et à renforcer sa passion pour la musique. Sa carrière professionnelle débute en 2017 avec la sortie du single « Sans défaut » au Ghana. Après une période consacrée à la création et à la recherche musicale entre le Nigeria et le Ghana, l’artiste revient en juillet 2025 avec « Bassinéré Sonh Sing-Néré ». Le titre lui permet de se produire sur plusieurs scènes au Burkina Faso et bénéficie d’une diffusion régulière dans les médias. Onze titres entre amour, patriotisme et résilience Avec « Baas-Néré », Joodal propose onze titres aux thématiques variées, dans lesquels l’amour occupe une place importante. L’album porte également un regard sur la situation du pays. Dans « Tond Min Paboogd'yéh », l’artiste rappelle la nécessité de se mobiliser lorsque la patrie traverse des difficultés. Le morceau rend aussi hommage aux Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) ainsi qu’aux Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP). Une identité musicale plurielle Sur le plan musical, « Baas-Néré » revendique une diversité de sonorités et de langues. L’afrobeat côtoie l’afrozouk et le highlife, tandis que les textes alternent entre le kassena, le mooré, le gourounsi et le français, avec quelques touches d’anglais. Enregistré entre le Ghana et le Nigeria, l’album porte ainsi l’empreinte des différentes influences rencontrées par l’artiste au cours de son parcours. Joodal présente sa musique comme une expression « fortement humaine », capable d’aider, d’apaiser, de motiver et de sensibiliser. Au-delà du divertissement, il entend faire de ses chansons un moyen de rapprocher les individus et de contribuer au rayonnement du Burkina Faso, « partout où besoin sera ». Avec « Baas-Néré », Joodal ouvre donc un nouveau chapitre de sa carrière. Après plusieurs années de construction artistique, ce premier album constitue une étape importante pour le chanteur. Son accueil par le public burkinabè et les professionnels de la musique permettra de mesurer la portée de cette nouvelle proposition artistique. items.title: Unease among Punjab police personnel on reports of deployment in KP
items.description: LAHORE: The concerns of the Punjab Police personnel, already facing issues of bad food and missing facilities during deployment in Rawalpindi division to counter the PTI march, further deepened on Sunday on the ‘rumours’ that 25,000 of the total 40,000 would be moved from Attock (Punjab) to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa after declaration of an emergency and imposition of the governor’s rule. Disillusioned by fatigue, lack of sleep and poor living conditions, a Punjab Police officer said, the exhausted police personnel were viewing the expected movement from Attock to KP as a new challenge and a serious trouble for them amid reports of poor facilities. During the last few weeks, there was a barrage of allegations surfacing against the Rawalpindi division police administration of supplying rotten and stale food to the deployed personnel while reports confirmed death of five policemen during the last two weeks in line of duty at Attock and Wah Cantt in connection with the PTI protest march. Two died of heart attacks, one drowned in a canal, two others died of medical complications while a constable was fighting for life after a snakebite in the jungle. As per the emerging reports, the police personnel have been complaining about the foul-smelling food, bad catering, poor washroom facilities and risky living conditions during the deployment, particularly in district Attock. IGP rejects reports, says no decision taken yet; 40,000 cops deployed to counter PTI march face lack of facilities, getting bad food; five lose life in line of duty Some senior officers also came to the support of their force and held the Rawalpindi police authorities responsible for the mismanagement. A senior officer said the videos recorded by the police personnel regarding the stale food continued to appear on social media with every passing day while the local police administration dubbed them merely ‘a conspiracy by some individual employees’ instead of resolving the problems. Some recordings showed insects or worms in food served to the force with personnel raising the issue. Most complaints were related to the foul-smelling food, poor catering and washroom facilities. Quoting some internal reports, the officer said that the Rawalpindi police top brass exchanged arguments with some senior officers of Punjab Police who highlighted the issue. The senior officers had arrived from other regions of the province to command their respective police force in Attock and Wah Cantt. About the deployment in KP, Punjab Inspector General of Police Abdul Kareem clarified that no final decision had been taken or any directive was issued for the relocation of the police force from Punjab to KP. “Although no final decision has been made yet to send the force to KP, if it happens, we will make it public officially,” he told Dawn . Regarding bad quality of food, he said steps to provide quality food to the force at Attock and Wah Cantt were being taken on a priority basis. He rejected the allegations of supply of adulterated food ‘on a large scale,’ terming the reports incorrect. “When complaints were inquired into, one of the police employees was caught mixing water in the food deliberately,” said Mr Kareem. Even then, he added, the Punjab Food Authority (PFA) had been tasked with checking the food quality and it had fielded teams to ensure provision of hygienic food and drinking water. The IGP confirmed the deaths of five personnel, saying, “Five police employees have lost their lives during the last two-week security deployment at Attock and Wah Cantt”. He identified them as constables Zulfiqar Ahmed, Zain Ali, Muhammad Imran, Muhammad Shahzad and Usman Idrees. “Two of them were martyred due to heart attack while one of them – Zain Ali - accidentally drowned after slipping into Ghazi Canal. The two other police personnel died in the line of duty due to severe medical complications,” the IG says. He rejected the reports about the death of a police employee by a snakebite, saying he was under treatment. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

9ᵉ édition du Maracana Garghin : Le trophée au champion, des vivres pour les plus démunis
items.description: Débutée le 5 juillet 2026 avec 24 équipes en compétition, la 9ᵉ édition du tournoi de Maracana Garghin a connu son épilogue ce 11 octobre 2026. La finale a opposé l'équipe de « La Jeunesse de Garghin » à celle des « Talents cachés de Cissin ». ​Au terme des deux mi-temps de 20 minutes, aucune des deux formations n'est parvenue à trouver le chemin des filets. C'est finalement à l'épreuve des tirs au but que les « Talents cachés de Cissin » se sont montrés les plus adroits, l’emportant 1 tir à 0. ​Selon le capitaine de l'équipe victorieuse, Amadé Sanfo, c'est avant tout la solidarité qui a guidé son groupe vers le sacre : « Il n'y a pas de secret. C'est la solidarité, le respect mutuel sur le terrain et l'écoute. Toutes les équipes étaient très fortes cette année » , a-t-il soutenu. ​Pour le promoteur de l'événement, le Dr Yves Kafando, cette 9ᵉ édition est une réussite totale. Un succès sur le terrain, où le niveau du jeu s'est révélé particulièrement élevé et empreint de fair-play, mais aussi en dehors du terrain grâce à l'appui des autorités. La présence de plusieurs membres du gouvernement à cette finale témoigne, selon lui, de l'intérêt porté au sport et à l'épanouissement de la jeunesse sous la Révolution Progressiste Populaire (RPP). ​Le promoteur a également tenu à exprimer sa gratitude aux FDS, aux VDP et au chef de l'État. « Je voudrais particulièrement vous demander, éminentes personnalités ici présentes, de traduire toute notre amitié et notre reconnaissance au camarade Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, grâce à qui nous pouvons nous réunir ce soir. Il y a quelques années, ce n'était pas évident lorsque la menace terroriste pesait sur Ouagadougou. Dites-lui que les fils et les filles de Garghin sont pleinement mobilisés pour répondre à son appel » , s'est-il adressé aux membres du gouvernement. ​Le mérite des différentes équipes engagées a été récompensé. L'équipe victorieuse, « Talents cachés de Cissin », est repartie avec le trophée, des médailles, une enveloppe de 750 000 F CFA, un jeu de maillots et quatre ballons. Le finaliste malheureux, « La Jeunesse de Garghin », s'est vu attribuer la somme de 500 000 F CFA, accompagnée de médailles, d'un jeu de maillots et de quatre ballons, tandis que la formation arrivée en troisième position a reçu 250 000 F CFA, un jeu de maillots et quatre ballons. ​Afin de magnifier la cohésion sociale et le vivre-ensemble, le prix du fair-play a été décerné à l'équipe « Espoir » pour son comportement exemplaire ; elle empoche ainsi 250 000 F CFA, un jeu de maillots et quatre ballons. Sur le plan individuel, le meilleur gardien et le meilleur buteur de la compétition ont reçu chacun un trophée, un téléphone portable et une somme de 50 000 F CFA. De son côté, le meilleur espoir du tournoi a également été distingué sous les yeux admiratifs de l'ambassadeur du sport, Charles Kaboré. ​Fidèle aux idéaux de la RPP, l'événement a aussi été marqué par un geste d'entraide communautaire. Un opérateur économique présent à la finale a décidé d'offrir séance tenante 200 sacs de riz aux personnes vulnérables de Garghin. Cette donation sera remise au chef du quartier qui en assurera la distribution. ​Dans ses perspectives, le Dr Yves Kafando souhaite faire du Maracana de Garghin une véritable pépinière capable de dénicher les futurs talents du football burkinabè. La présence de Charles Kaboré traduisait d'ailleurs cette ambition. En ouverture de la finale, le public a pu assister à un match de gala au cours duquel les anciennes gloires du football national se sont imposées face à une équipe de Garghin grâce à un doublé de l'ambassadeur du sport. items.title: Peshawar becomes city of containers
items.description: PESHAWAR: Despite being in throes of violence for the past many decades, Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, has most of the time enjoyed political stability. The violence came and went but political stability was always there despite the sabre-rattling with federal government and marches on Islamabad. A semblance of understanding between Islamabad and Peshawar, no matter how little, was still there. However, all this changed on Sunday after the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the province. The night before, skies of Peshawar poured buckets, flooding roads and drenching the city; however, the Sunday morning was warm and sunny. Yet it started with a sense of dread as uncertainty hung heavy over the city. The telltale signs of not everything is good dawned upon after reaching for telephone, the ritual everyone does upon waking up. The impending doom was there for all to see: no mobile signals. Routine journey in the city turns into hectic exercise as governor’s rule imposed The city had witnessed a nearly 48 hours long mobile service blackout just days ago owing to PTI protest march. Outside, the stations of Peshawar Bus Transit (BRT), whose buses come on road early in the morning, remained shut. The GT Road was closed at Firdous Chowk by placing shipping containers. A large number of police personnel was deputed at this spot. Only pedestrians were allowed to move ahead on GT Road and a large number of cops were sitting outside the shuttered shops on GT Road between Hospital Road and Firdous Chowk, also called the Malik Saad Shaheed Chowk. A bearded cop on the road stopped me and handed over a shopping bag containing fried peas. Perplexed, I looked at him and he turned his back toward me, asking me to put the peas into the back pocket of his bulletproof vest. The gates of Bala Hisar Fort, which houses the headquarters of Frontier Corps North, were shuttered and a contingent of policemen was resting on the footpath. A few steps from here just outside the KP Assembly is Surey Chowk, from where GT Road leads commuters to Khyber Road, which houses the city red zone. Police guard a road leading to the Red Zone, in Peshawar. — Reuters The road leading to Khyber Road was blocked with containers and the gate erected to control traffic was also closed. A large number of cops were milling around Surey Pul Square, which is the most favoured spot for protesters of all kinds and hues. At the end of Justice Rustam Kiyani Road near central jail , where the artery leads to Sher Shah Suri Road, an old armoured personnel carrier was parked and two cops there were telling walkers not to proceed further. A few of us ignored their warnings but just next to MPA Hostel, a large contingent of cops yelled at us to go back and take detour through Shoba Bazaar. The Jail Pul, which connects Sher Shah Suri Road with Khyber Bazaar, was also closed. I met an acquaintance there who offered to take me through Civil Secretariat and we entered the Police Road and secretariat without any hassle. Civil Secretariat, the beating heart of KP government, was completely deserted with a few cars parked outside the chief secretary office. On Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum Road, where houses of minister and governor are located, security was very tight and police personnel were checking everyone heading towards both the houses. From the distance, I saw a large number of vehicles parked outside the Governor’s Houses. Walking the road in the opposite direction towards Khyber Road, I saw an APC, a prison van and truck carrying riot police, heading in the direction of Chief Minister House. After a few minutes’ walk, a barricade was erected on Khyber Road near Army Stadium and when I approached the personnel standing there and explained that I needed to cross to the other side, a plainclothes youth holding a radio just sputtered a series of “no, no, no, no. You must go back. This road is closed and we cannot open this barrier.” I stood there in plain confusion thinking of what to do. No question of going back and with no telephone, I was unable to approach any official. Then as a last resort, I pleaded with paramilitary personnel to let me out and one of them signalled another guard to open the gate for me. But the plainclothes again jumped in front of me and said no. Then the other, standing behind laughed, perhaps, they were enjoying my confusion or saw fear on my face. “How rudimentary freedom is,” muses one of the characters in JM Coetzee. Waiting for the Barbarians. Little did we realise how important is the ability to move freely without any fear, without being stopped. Outside the stretch of Khyber Road, connecting University Road and Airport Road, Amn Chowk was open but there was little traffic. A large contingent of cops was present at Amn Chowk, previously called the Gora Qabristan Chowk. The University Road was blocked at Tehkal with containers, a biker told me. There were also containers on Stadium Chowk only letting cars in a single line on both sides. Saddar Bazaar was partially open oblivious to changing political fortunes and game of thrones which was currently under way just a stone’s throw away. A container was also placed on Arbab Road, connecting Mall Road to Saddar Road, with a few cops lazing under a tree outside the Presentation Convent School. For many years, marchers from Peshawar used to result into turning the federal capital into a fortress of containers but this time Islamabad instead sent containers to Peshawar. It is to be seen how long these containers are going to stay here. In the afternoon, the internet also died. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

items.title: Senegal: Brutal Crackdown Violates LGBT People’s Rights
items.description: Click to expand Image Renovated Dakar Railway station inaugurated, May 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch Senegal’s intensifying crackdown on LGBT people is violating their rights and causing increasing fear and stigma. Fear of arrest and stigma are causing people to go into hiding, to avoid HIV testing and treatment, and deterring lawyers from representing them. The crackdown on LGBT people calls into question Senegal’s compliance with its own laws and international law, as well as the Olympic charter, given it will host the Youth Olympics Games at the end of the month. (Dakar) Senegal’s growing crackdown on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) people is violating their rights, causing increasing fear and stigma, and should be ended immediately, Human Rights Watch said today. Mass arrests forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation appear to be part of an increase in punitive government action against LGBT people in West Africa. On March 11, 2026, Senegal’s parliament amended article 319 of the penal code, doubling to 10 years the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex conduct and criminalizing “promotion” of or support to LGBT people and organizations. The amendment followed the detention by security forces of at least five men in Thiès region in December 2025 and 12 men in the capital, Dakar, in February 2026 on charges including “acts against nature” and “intentional transmission of HIV.” Police and gendarmerie then escalated arrests of suspected LGBT people in various other cities including Thiès, Rosso, Saint Louis, Yeumbeul, and Ziguinchor. “LGBT people are being forced to curb their normal activities and to keep from exercising their rights for fear of arrest and increased stigma,” said Larissa Kojoué, LGBT rights researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 39 people in May in Senegal: 5 people who had been detained in late 2025 and early 2026, 2 journalists, 9 civil society representatives and human rights defenders, 2 national officials, 2 lawyers, 4 health professionals, and 15 members of the Senegalese queer community. Human Rights Watch also reviewed official statements, and media and nongovernmental group reports. On September 29, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Senegalese authorities, including the justice minister, the high commander of the National Gendarmerie and director of military justice, and the director general of the National Police detailing its findings and asking specific questions, but has received no response. Same-sex sexual conduct has been criminalized in Senegal since 1965, but hostility toward LGBT people has significantly intensified in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Diomaye Faye and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko pledged to strengthen laws criminalizing same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority and mobilizing broad political and public support. The March amendments have triggered new attacks against LGBT people, interviewees said. Mouhamadou Seck, secretary-general of the prominent Senegalese organization African Forum for the Defense of Human Rights (Rencontre Africaine pour la Défense des Droits de l’Homme, or RADDHO), said in May that “detentions, violence, and abuse against LGBT individuals have sharply increased across the country.” Human Rights Watch was not able to independently verify the total number of arrests linked to article 319. However, between February and July, at least 212 people have been arrested, according to data collected by RADDHO. HIV Justice Network reported that the number of arrests exceeded more than 300 during the same period. Of those arrested, 82 were also charged with “voluntary HIV transmission,” although a court dismissed these charges in August. These figures illustrate the scale of arrests and indicate a pattern in enforcement of article 319. Security force officials have stated that they have arrested people suspected of engaging in same-sex conduct based on information extracted from previously seized phones, third-party allegations, or raids on private premises. The March amendment to the penal code introduces broadly defined offenses criminalizing activities such as “promotion” and “glorification” of homosexuality, as well as financing and supporting LGBT individuals and organizations. Human rights defenders and lawyers said that the introduction of these offenses has led to fear and anxiety among legal professionals and contributed to an environment in which detainees struggle to secure legal representation. “In Senegal, lawyers are associated with the cause they represent,” a lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch, adding that his colleagues and family members had urged him not to represent individuals arrested on charges of “acts against nature.” He said: “Everyone has the right to a fair trial. What matters to me is: were their rights respected or not?” Principle 18 of the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers provides that “Lawyers shall not be identified with their clients or their clients’ causes as a result of discharging their functions.” People interviewed said that since February, the authorities have subjected detainees to HIV testing without informed consent and used detainees’ HIV status to justify additional criminal charges or prolonged detention. Health professionals expressed concern that the forced HIV testing and subsequent charges undermine medical confidentiality by allowing confidential test results to be used in criminal proceedings. They also discourage people from seeking HIV testing and treatment and jeopardize HIV-related public health efforts. “We have noticed that […] some people have fled while others are hiding,” a doctor in Dakar said. “One-third no longer come in for appointments to seek HIV treatment.” Security forces also appear to have violated the confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBT people. News reporting on two cases involving public figures includes personal details that closely track details set forth in investigative records, suggesting authorities leaked confidential information to journalists. Local media also extensively reported personal and confidential data on the case of the 12 men arrested in February. This has exposed individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats, and violence. The Senegalese Constitution and international human rights law applicable in Senegal guarantee fundamental rights, including equal protection before the law and non-discrimination; the right to effective legal representation and the presumption of innocence; the rights to privacy and to informed consent to medical treatment; freedom from torture and other ill-treatment, and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. Senegal’s Law No. 2010-03 of April 9, 2010, on HIV/AIDS establishes a legal framework to ensure access to treatment and support and protect the rights of people living with or affected by HIV. The law guarantees the rights to informed consent in medical testing and to privacy and confidentiality of health information, as well as protection against discrimination based on HIV status and protection of detainees from mandatory HIV testing. The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, ratified by Senegal in 1982, guarantees, among other rights, the right to a fair trial, to equal protection before the law, and to nondiscrimination. The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, which will meet in Dakar from October 12–21, explicitly called on member states, including Senegal, to protect sexual minorities in accordance with the African charter, and has urged governments to protect people from violence based on their sexual orientation and gender identity. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Senegal is a party, requires Senegal to ensure the protection of numerous rights including fair trial, equal protection, nondiscrimination, and the right to privacy. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, has repeatedly held that the criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct between adults violates the covenant. From October 31 to November 13, Senegal will host the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event on the African continent. The Olympic Charter prohibits discrimination on any grounds and commits host countries to respect human rights and human dignity. “The ongoing government crackdown on LGBT people raises serious concerns about Senegal’s compliance with international law, the Olympic charter, and Senegal’s own laws,” Kojoué said. “The government should call a halt to this crackdown.” Click to expand Image Interview with Sall (pseudonym), university student in Dakar, Senegal, who has barely left his room since February due to stigma and fear of arrest, May 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch Expanded Criminalization of Same-Sex Conduct On March 11, Senegal’s Parliament adopted amendments to article 319 of the penal code by a vote of 135 to 0, with three abstentions. The new law doubles, to 10 years, the maximum prison term for same-sex conduct and increases fines from 2 million to 10 million CFA francs (roughly US$3,000 to US$17,000). The law introduces penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5 million CFA ($850 to $8,500) for those accused of promoting homosexuality or supporting or financing LGBT persons and organizations. It also instructs judges not to suspend sentences or reduce prison terms below the minimum penalty recommended. Arbitrary Arrest, Detention According to data from July by the HIV Justice Network, since early February, authorities “have arrested over 300 individuals on allegations of acts against nature” in cities across Senegal. Data collected by RADDHO shows 212 people were arrested between February and July. RADDHO told Human Rights Watch that their data indicates that gendarmes from the Keur Massar unit carried out the majority of the arrests. Keur Massar is about 25 kilometers east of downtown Dakar. On June 25, Keur Massar district gendarmerie arrested the 101st suspect in connection with the arrest wave that began in February, according to media reports. Officers said the arrests followed their review of a mobile phone seized from one of the 12 men arrested in February. In July 30, international media reported that Keur Massar gendarmes arrested eight women who have been placed in pretrial detention. The gendarmes used phone data from two who were allegedly in a relationship to identify and arrest the six others. Beside “acts against nature,” investigators also cited allegations of pimping, corruption of minors, and drug-related offenses. Police in the Thiès region, about 70 km east of Dakar, arrested five men in December 2025 for smoking shisha, a tobacco product banned under local law, and held them for two days before presenting them to a judicial authority. The prosecutor ordered them held on charges of “acts against nature” but dropped the charges and released them a month later for lack of evidence. They said that they believe neighbors denounced them to the authorities because of their sexual orientation. One of the five, a 23-year-old man, said: We were arrested while preparing for a fashion show at my place. Around 9 p.m., three police officers arrived, took us to the station and confiscated our phones.… We were held for two days, then taken to the Thiès prosecutor’s office and charged with acts against nature, despite not being caught in the act.… I think our neighbors told the police we are gay because they were jealous of our successful fashion business. He said that, “we were beaten, whipped, and slapped, and called homosexuals.... I was injured on my thigh, causing lasting pain.” A social worker operating in Rebeuss, Senegal’s largest detention facility, located in Dakar, said he witnessed prison staff and detainees discriminate against those held on suspicion of homosexuality: “[LGBT detainees] are being excluded from communal activities, denied participation in collective prayer sessions, and required to access services, including the barber, separately from other prisoners. In some cases, they are even compelled to perform domestic labor.” Prolonged Pretrial Detention Since February, only one person arrested for “acts against nature” has been convicted according to local media. On April 10, the Pikine-Guédiawaye District Court, in a suburb of Dakar, sentenced a 24-year-old man, who had been arrested a week earlier, to six years in prison and imposed a fine of 2 million CFA franc (approximately $3,300) after convicting him of “acts against nature” and “public indecency.” He was not represented by legal counsel as it is often the case for people accused of “acts against nature” who may be denied access to legal representation or face difficulty finding lawyers willing to represent them. A lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch that many of those arrested on homosexuality-related charges remain in pretrial detention because prosecutors have added supplementary charges, including criminal association, endangering the life of others, deliberate HIV transmission, and drug trafficking. The lawyer said that these additional charges often require longer investigations and are used to justify extending pretrial detention. Senegalese law generally limits pretrial detention to six months for minor offenses, with no limit for certain serious crimes such as murder, offenses against state security, and embezzlement of public funds. International human rights law requires that pretrial detention should be an exception, not the rule, and be justified on an individual basis in every case. Anyone held in pretrial detention is entitled to a trial within a reasonable time or release. Lengthy pretrial detention remains a significant concern in Senegal, as several civil society organizations and government officials interviewed said. On August 7, the Pikine-Guediawaye District Court officially closed the preliminary investigation into the case involving the 12 men arrested on February 9 and another 87 people arrested in connection with the same crackdown. The court dismissed cases for 28 and freed them, but 71 remain referred to trial on charges of criminal association and acts against nature. The district court also dismissed charges of “endangering other people’s lives” and “voluntary HIV transmission.” This decision raises questions regarding continued detention of the 12 accused as the investigative needs that are commonly invoked to justify prolonged pretrial detention may no longer apply. Barriers to Legal Representation Human Rights Watch found that that the newly introduced offense of “promotion of homosexuality” has had a chilling effect on access to legal representation. Lawyers and human rights defenders said they were concerned that representing people charged under article 319 could expose them to professional, social, or even legal repercussions. “How can we represent people arrested without being accused of promotion,” one lawyer said. “That’s why there is such strong reluctance.” The lawyer described serious obstacles to accessing legal representation, saying that detainees, including his own client, were pressured to waive their right to legal representation. He also said that authorities frequently questioned detainees and obtained statements in the absence of legal counsel. On February 9, the lawyer filed two complaints before the Dakar Court of Appeals, one on his own behalf and one on behalf of his client against a gendarmerie commander who pressured his client to waive his right to legal representation. He said in September that no progress had been made in either case. Another lawyer raised concern about gendarmes’ respect for due process. He suspected that authorities had obtained his clients “confessions” without their fully understanding of the proceedings and the implications of their statements. Forced HIV Testing; Disclosure of Medical Information RADDHO and HIV Justice Network told Human Rights Watch that the authorities have forced most detainees to undergo HIV testing and, when the results were positive, charged them with “deliberate HIV transmission” and “endangering the lives of others” in addition to offenses under article 319 of the amended penal code. Under article 36 of Senegal’s 2010 law on HIV/AIDS, anyone who is knowingly living with HIV and has unprotected sex may face 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine. The Keur Massar gendarmerie has officially stated that they required arrested people to undergo HIV tests. The national police also have conducted such tests and used the HIV status in criminal proceedings, as they mentioned in their June 13 statement. “We are aware about nonconsensual HIV testing by gendarmerie and disclosure of people’s HIV status,” a doctor told Human Rights Watch. The consequences of these practices have extended beyond individual detainees. Health professionals said that the use of HIV-related services has sharply declined and attribute it to fear of arrest, forced disclosure, and social stigma. “If, because of the law, people decide to stop coming to health clinics, it becomes a public health problem,” a doctor said. The Public Health Ministry and the National Council for the Fight Against AIDS (Conseil National de Lutte Contre le Sida, or CNLS), a government body leading and coordinating the HIV response in Senegal, released joint statements on Facebook on February 11 and February 23 stressing national efforts to treat and prevent HIV/AIDS and support people living with HIV/AIDS, as well as the need to keep medical and judicial records separate, and the difficulty of establishing intentional transmission. In a March 18 news statement, the Joint UN Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), which advocates for global action against the HIV/AIDS pandemic, expressed concerns over the impact of the amended law, and called on Senegal to protect the confidentiality of medical information and the patient-provider relationship as non-negotiable foundations of a functioning health system. Breaches of Privacy and Confidentiality Numerous local media reports on the recent cases include highly detailed personal information about individuals arrested by the security forces. In at least four cases, the information closely tracks information in case records, nearly verbatim, suggesting that confidential information was being directly shared with journalists. “Our photos and items found [by Police] at my home, like lubricants and antiretroviral tablets, were published in newspapers and on social media,” the 23-year-old man said. In one prominent case, a rare instance in which the detainee had legal representation after his arrest, Keur Massar gendarmes detained a popular artist on charges of “acts against nature,” and his name, HIV status, and other confidential information appeared soon afterward in the media. As a Senegalese journalist put it: “Publishing ‘scandalous’ information, on such a taboo matter like homosexuality in Senegal, has increasingly become a means of driving audience engagement. This practice turns people’s suffering into spectacle, with little regard for the serious consequences for those whose privacy and dignity are violated.” Mental Health Consequences of the Crackdown The government crackdown has had serious social and psychological effects on LGBT people across the country. LGBT individuals interviewed said they experienced fear, anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts, and many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements, withdrawn from social and online life, relocated, or abandoned mobile phones to avoid detection by the security forces. A 22-year-old university student said he was forced to move after facing verbal threats and harassment: In the neighborhood where I was, people started insulting me. They would say things like ‘next time it is your turn,’ when I passed [by them]. Kids would even follow me singing ‘goor-jigeen’ [a Wolof word describing a man who appears and behaves like a woman] and adults would say nothing. I couldn’t even defend myself. I knew if I said something, they would all come after me. To come back home I had to wait until it is dark so no one would notice me. A 27-year-old community worker in Dakar, said constant fear has turned daily life “into a state resembling COVID confinement”: We have suspended all our activities, including online. Now nobody trusts anyone. There is a total lack of security. I know I have one foot in prison. I can be arrested anytime because I am a community leader. Even if I am not in prison right now, I live like I am in prison. Life has totally changed. Another 21-year-old man among those arrested in December 2025 said that, following his release in January 2026, he has been living in hiding in central Senegal, unable to return home out of fear his relatives would assault him: I received a call from my mother telling me not to come back home. Apparently, my [half] brothers and some of my cousins were waiting for me and [were] ready to teach me a lesson. I have been hiding since. I couldn’t even go back home to pick up some stuff. I have withdrawn from several online groups and deactivated my social media. Many of my friends left for Gambia, Mauritania, or Morrocco. I am staying because I am my mother’s only child. A 35-year-old man in Ziguinchor said his partner left with no prior notice for a neighboring country causing him psychological distress: My partner left the country at night on a motorbike when he heard that his close friends were arrested and the police raided his place. He threw away his phone. He lives in poor conditions on the other side of the border. He does not have his medication. I am scared for him. A psychologist at Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar said that her consultations on campus “have tripled” since March. “Many patients are young men experiencing severe anxiety, hypervigilance, withdrawal from social life, and obsessive behaviors driven by fear of being perceived and attacked as LGBT.” Recommendations To Senegal’s President Order the immediate release of everyone arbitrarily detained since February 2026 under article 319 of the penal code. Refer the amended law to the Constitutional Council for constitutional review of its compatibility with constitutional guarantees of the right to privacy, equality before the law, non-discrimination, and fair trial rights. Publicly commit, ahead of the Youth Olympic Games, to ensure that all participants, visitors, and residents alike, will be protected from discrimination and arbitrary arrests. To the National Assembly Repeal article 319 in its entirety, including the provisions of the amended penal code that criminalize the “promotion” or “glorification” of homosexuality, as well as the financing or support of LGBT individuals and organizations.Initiate a legislative review to remove HIV status as a criminal aggravating factor. To Senegal’s Government Open an investigation of abuses documented against LGBT people and hold those responsible accountable.Instruct judicial authorities to uphold national and international laws to guarantee access to legal representation for all detainees and ensure lawyers can represent clients without intimidation, harassment, or risk of prosecution.Ensure that pretrial detention is an exceptional measure, not a standard procedure, and that anyone in such detention is guaranteed a trial within a reasonable time or release.Prohibit forced HIV testing, ensure informed consent for all medical testing, prevent the use of confidential health information in criminal proceedings, and protect medical confidentiality, including by prohibiting the disclosure of detainees’ health information to the media.Open an independent investigation into the case concerning a gendarmerie commander who pressured a detainee to waive his right to legal representation before leaking the detainee’s HIV status to journalists.Respect and protect the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly, including for individuals and organizations advocating for the rights of LGBT people. To the National Medical Council Reaffirm that forced HIV testing violates medical ethics.

items.title: Due to high cost, 25pc of cancer patients at Karachi's JPMC abandon treatment, experts say
items.description: KARACHI: Around 25 per cent of cancer patients at the Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC) are unable to complete their treatment, speakers said on the concluding day of a two-day conference, attributing the situation to the high cost of newer therapies and inconsistent philanthropic assistance. The event titled Breastcon 2026 was organised by JPMC. According to speakers, while the province’s largest tertiary-care public-sector hospital offers surgery and radiotherapy free of charge, the high costs of newer immunotherapies and targeted therapies force many patients to discontinue treatment. Regretting the situation, JPMC’s head of the oncology department, Dr Ghulam Haider, called for permanent government assistance to help patients complete treatment. Complete cancer care costs Rs3-4m, with many patients unable to afford newer therapies, says oncology dept head “Cancer care at JPMC is supported by philanthropists, charities and Zakat funds, but this assistance is not consistently available. Gaps in medicine supplies and funding can interrupt treatment and affect its outcomes,” he said, emphasising that reliance on charitable donations alone was insufficient. According to him, the overall cost of complete cancer care, including surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and injections, ranges from Rs3 million to Rs4m. The management of complications arising from chemotherapy can further increase costs. “Some patients return home after exhausting their resources and come back months later with larger tumours,” he told the audience. JPMC assistant professor of medical oncology Dr Saima Zahoor, who was also the conference co-chair, said that more than 60pc of breast cancer patients faced delays in diagnosis or treatment. “Social pressure, fear, misconceptions and treatment costs contribute to these delays. Others fear [that a] biopsy will spread cancer and turn to alternative treatments, losing months before reaching a hospital,” she lamented. She also spoke about HER2-positive breast cancer, an aggressive form of the disease in which cells produce excessive amounts of the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) protein, causing tumours to grow and divide faster. She said the condition might require expensive targeted medicines. At the same time, seeking assistance from Baitul Mal or charities could further delay care. “Women should consult a qualified doctor about unusual breast changes. Early diagnosis and timely treatment improve the chances of recovery,” she noted. JPMC general surgeon Dr Syeda Zareen Raza said that some patients could undergo breast conservation or oncoplastic surgery, adding that fears about appearance, hair loss and social attitudes could discourage them from seeking treatment. Dr Sana Zeeshan of Aga Khan University Hospital called for a national breast cancer registry that combines records from public, private, and charitable hospitals. Data on disease stages, treatment, recurrence and survival would help identify gaps and guide research, she said. Dr Najeeb Naimatullah of Shaukat Khanum Hospital called for organised screening, access to quality local and generic medicines and consideration of patients’ financial circumstances in treatment. Chief guest Dr Tariq Rafi, chairman of the Sindh Higher Education Commission, urged stronger screening, cooperation between institutions and medical research, while offering the commission’s support to researchers through available funding. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

items.title: Citizens protest against what is being built ‘in secret’ at Karachi's Nehr-i-Khayam
items.description: KARACHI: Environmentalists and residents from across the city, including Clifton Block 5 Residents Association, Clifton Defence Com­munity (CDC) and Karachi Resi­dents’ Community (District South), gathered at the construction site of Nehr-i-Khayam on Sunday to protest the building of a commercial belt there. Standing firm against the backdrop of a big yellow digger machine hard at work and a reversing concrete mixer truck, the protesters held up placards with messages such as ‘Violation of Supreme Court orders’, ‘No food street on Nehr-i-Khayam’, ‘What are you building? Share the plan publicly’, ‘Don’t suffocate our waterways’, ‘Narrow drain equals massive flood’, ‘Boat Basin Se Gutter Basin’, etc. Founder and CEO of the Clifton Urban Forest, environmentalist Masood Lohar lamented people who call themselves architects, engineers and town planners but don’t really know what they are doing. “Nehr-i-Khayam is a natural link between the Obhayo Lagoon and the Gizri Creek. You can’t mess up with the marine ecosystem. If you do, you brace yourselves for floods, storms and tsunamis,” he pointed out. Quoting the late Dawn columnist and social activist Ardeshir Cowasjee from his column published on Sept 10, 2006, one of the protesters and members of the Karachi Residents’ Community (District South), Rasha Tarek, said that he had called Nehr-i-Khayam “one of the major lungs of the Clifton area”, intended “to carry rain and/or tidal water and not sewage into the open sea”. Environmentalists, activists gather at construction site; say protecting city’s drainage infrastructure, channels, open banks is everyone’s concern Reminding the gathering that Nehr-i-Khayam is an integral part of Boat Basin and Karachi’s drainage infrastructure and that its channel, open banks and surrounding landscape are shared public assets whose protection concerns the entire city, she demanded an immediate stop to the ongoing construction, which would narrow and alter the channel and its banks. Rumana Khan, another protester, said that the people of this country are bearing the brunt of wrong decisions made by the government in the past too. “For instance, building dams in all the wrong places while restricting the natural flow of rivers. Then you get flash floods that destroy villages and settlements,” she said. Hummaa Ahmad, who lives in the vicinity, wondered how come a seemingly big commercial project such as this has no public project information board installed anywhere. “We want to know exactly what is being constructed here. We want full disclosure of the approved designs, land boundaries, environmental assessments, Sepa decisions, contracts and expenditure regarding the project,” she demanded. “It is illegal commercialisation,” said another protester Sheeraz Qureshi, whose family has resided in Clifton Block 5 for the last 40 years. “You cannot build a dense commercial area in the middle of a dense residential area. That way you disturb all the residents,” he said. Echoing him, Dr Nadia Kiran, a resident of one of the apartments overlooking Nehr-i-Khayam, said, “We have heard that they are going to narrow the drain and build a food street over it. “The resulting traffic, rush and noise every day and night will dest­roy our peace of mind,” she added. “As it is, the authorities look the other way while allowing untreated waste to flow to the sea through drains such as Nehr-i-Khayam while overlooking the negative impacts of it on marine life,” said Humaira Khan of the Clifton Defence Commu­nity and Clifton Block 5 Residents Association. “Whatever way you see it, it is encroachment, plain and simple! Build­ing commercial belts is not the job of the Sindh government, which should be more concerned about saving the environment than contributing towards destroying it,” she said. CDC President Abdur Rehman pointed out that there have been previous attempts to encroach on Nehr-i-Khayam, too. “Basically, it seems that it is the government’s priority to make money one way or the other,” he said. “Water streams or flowing waterways anywhere should be seen as a gift of nature but sadly we love to encroach upon them or constrict the flow. We are constructing roads and big buildings but for some strange reason we don’t build a proper infrastructure for the flow of water, be it clean or sewage water. Lyari River and Malir River are sitting examples of the ill-will of our rulers. Then when the city drowns after a little bit of rain they say ‘more rain means more water’,” he shrugged. The protesters, who also included Elia Qazil­bash, Syed Tipu Sharif, Shumaila Daw­ood, also demanded full financial disclosure of the project, said to be announced at Rs500 million. They said that this must include the approved budget, funding sources, contract scope, contractors, payments and actual expenditure. Their further demands included protection of the channel’s storm-water cap­a­city and public open space, no shops, food street or other commercial encroachment on the cha­nnel land, proper sewage treatment before discha­rging wastewater into the sea and an independent scrutiny of drainage and environmental impa­cts and meaningful public con­sultation before any decision on further works. When contacted, a KMC spokesperson told Dawn that the project was being executed by the local government department and it had nothing to do with the KMC or Karachi mayor. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

items.title: Morocco Royal Tour (étape de Rabat) : Le Maroc vice-champion de la Coupe des Nations
items.description: L'équipe nationale du Maroc d'équitation a décroché, dimanche soir, la deuxième place de la Coupe des Nations 2026 de saut d'obstacles, dans le cadre de la 2è étape de la 15ème édition du Morocco Royal Tour, organisée au Royal Complexe des sports équestres et Tbourida Dar Essalam, sous le Haut Patronage due Roi Mohammed VI. L'équipe du Maroc a terminé à la 2è place à l'issue d’une épreuve de barrage remportée par la France, après que les deux sélections, ainsi que l'Allemagne et la Belgique, ont été à égalité de points de pénalité au terme des première et deuxième manches. Cette compétition s'est disputée sur des obstacles d'une hauteur de 1,50 mètre, dans la catégorie quatre étoiles (CSIO4*-W), et comptait pour le prix du ministère de l'Éducation nationale, du préscolaire et des sports. Le titre de la Coupe des Nations est revenu à l'équipe française, composée d'Olivier Perreau, Alix Ragot, Cyril Bouvard et Jeanne Sadran, qui a bouclé les deux manches avec un total de quatre points de pénalité. La cavalière Jeanne Sadran, montant le cheval « Dexter de Kerglenn », a ensuite remporté le barrage sans faute avec un chronomètre de 33.24/100è. De son côté, le cavalier marocain Abdelkebir Ouaddar, en selle sur « Festival d'Argouges », a réussi un parcours sans faute en 33.78/100è, offrant ainsi la deuxième place à l'équipe du Maroc, composée de Ali Al Ahrach, El Ghali Boukaa, Abdelkebir Ouaddar et Abdeslam Bennani Smires, qui avaient achevé la première manche avec quatre points de pénalité avant de signer un parcours sans faute lors de la deuxième manche. L'équipe de l’Allemagne, composée de Marie Ligges, Harm Lahde, Tom Schewe et Maximilian Lill, s'est classée troisième après avoir totalisé quatre points de pénalité sur les deux manches, avant que le cavalier Tom Schewe ne réalise un parcours sans faute au barrage en 34.93/100è. Dans une déclaration à la presse, l'entraîneur de l'équipe nationale de saut d'obstacles, Philippe Rozier, a exprimé sa satisfaction du classement des cavaliers marocains en Coupe des Nations, soulignant que ce résultat constitue une étape importante vers la réalisation des objectifs fixés pour la sélection nationale. Il a précisé que l'ambition de l'équipe du Maroc pour la troisième et dernière étape du Morocco Royal Tour, prévue à El Jadida, est de remporter le Grand Prix par l'intermédiaire de l'un des quatre cavaliers marocains, soulignant la difficulté de passer d'une compétition quatre étoiles à une cinq étoiles, ainsi que la transition d'une piste extérieure à une salle couverte. Il a fait savoir que les quatre chevaux ayant participé à la Coupe des Nations possèdent des qualités exceptionnelles, considérant que le maintien de leur condition physique sera essentiel pour continuer à rivaliser au plus haut niveau. Pour sa part, le cavalier marocain Ali Al Ahrach s'est réjoui de cette deuxième place, indiquant que l'objectif de l'équipe nationale était de remporter le titre, mais que la place de vice-champion demeure un résultat très satisfaisant. Il a salué les efforts déployés par l'ensemble des membres de l'équipe nationale pour atteindre cette performance, espérant faire encore mieux lors de la prochaine édition, malgré la rude concurrence attendue. L'entraîneur de l'équipe de France, Olivier Guillon, a, quant à lui, salué la prestation du cavalier marocain Abdelkebir Ouaddar lors du barrage, soulignant que son départ en première position et son temps très rapide ont mis une forte pression sur les quatre équipes en lice pour le titre. Il a expliqué que le staff technique français avait suivi de près le parcours d'Abdelkebir Ouaddar pour identifier les zones de piste afin de gagner des fractions de seconde, ajoutant que la cavalière française Jeanne Sadran a parfaitement appliqué cette stratégie en livrant une performance exceptionnelle qui a permis à la France de s'adjuger le titre. Le cavalier marocain, Abdelkebir Ouaddar, montant « Larsino », s'était illustré, plus tôt dans la journée, en décrochant la troisième place du Prix de la Société Royale d'Encouragement du Cheval (SOREC), une épreuve quatre étoiles, disputée sur des obstacles de 1,45 mètre, avec un chrono de 46.89/100è et un sans-faute. Avec l'épreuve de la Coupe des Nations, le rideau est tombé sur la deuxième étape du Morocco Royal Tour de saut d'obstacles, qui avait débuté à Tétouan (1er-4 octobre), et qui connaîtra son dénouement à El Jadida (15-18 octobre), dans le cadre du Salon du Cheval. The post Morocco Royal Tour (étape de Rabat) : Le Maroc vice-champion de la Coupe des Nations appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: UN: Burundi Set to Win Human Rights Council Seat Despite Abuses
items.description: Click to expand Image Burundi's President Evariste Ndayishimiye speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, in New York, New York, September 23, 2026. © 2026 AP Photo/Heather Khalifa (New York) – Burundi is set to win re-election to the United Nations Human Rights Council in a vote on October 12, 2026, with no competition, Human Rights Watch said today. Burundi is seeking to retain its seat even though the government of this Central African country has not improved its abusive human rights conditions. Burundi is one of the four African countries running for the same number of seats on the 47-nation council. The regional slates for the Western group, Latin America and the Caribbean, Central and Eastern Europe, and Asia also lack competition. This effectively guarantees all 15 candidates, fit or unfit, spots on the UN’s premier rights body for three years beginning on January 1, 2027. “This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word ‘election,’” said Louis Charbonneau, UN director at Human Rights Watch. “UN member states should insist on competitive slates so they can reject candidates with poor human rights records. No one should have a seat on this crucial body handed to them on a silver platter.” Ghana, Nigeria, and Zambia are candidates for Africa’s other three available seats. In Asia, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, and Nepal are running for the region’s four seats. In Latin America and the Caribbean, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and Uruguay are set to take the region’s three spots. For the Western group, Germany and Ireland are on track to get the group’s two available seats, while Moldova and Ukraine will take Central and Eastern Europe’s two spots. Despite some positive government statements, Burundi has not carried out meaningful reform to address longstanding concerns related to governance, justice, or accountability. Grave abuses persist with impunity, including extrajudicial executions, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, and detention. Freedom of expression, assembly, and association remain severely restricted. Burundi is in the third year of its current term and is allowed to run for another consecutive term. On October 6, the country’s delegation tried to use their membership to prevent UN scrutiny of Burundi’s poor human rights record, first by calling a vote to renew the mandate of the UN special rapporteur on Burundi and then by voting against it. The resolution was adopted, though, 22 to 7, with 17 abstentions. That resolution not only expressed concerns about ongoing rights violations but highlighted Burundi’s refusal to cooperate with the council and most of its mechanisms, including the special rapporteur. General Assembly Resolution 60/251, which created the Human Rights Council in 2006, says that countries voting for members should “take into account the contribution of candidates to the promotion and protection of human rights.” Council members are required to “uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights” at home and abroad and to “fully cooperate with the Council.” Candidates only need a simple majority in the secret-ballot vote in the 193-nation General Assembly to secure a seat on the Human Rights Council. That makes it highly unlikely that any candidate will lose, no matter how unqualified. Nevertheless, UN member states should not cast votes for abusive governments that are demonstrably unqualified for council membership. Among the other candidates, Nigeria should ensure accountability for serious international crimes committed by all parties—including security forces—during the conflict with the armed group Boko Haram. Brazil should investigate and curb police abuse after law enforcement officers set a grim record in 2025 by killing more than 6,500 people, the vast majority of them Black. Ukraine has suffered countless atrocities committed by Russian forces on its territory since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. At the same time, Ukrainian authorities have unjustly prosecuted Ukrainian civilians living under Russian occupation, including teachers, medics, municipal workers, and volunteers for doing essential work that international humanitarian law permits civilians to perform under occupation. The Human Rights Council scrutinizes all UN member states’ rights records in the Universal Periodic Review process. In November 2025, the United States refused to participate in its review. If the US government does not participate in its rescheduled review in November, it will become the first member country not to complete its review. The Human Rights Council has played a crucial role in ensuring independent investigations of abuses in Syria, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Ukraine, Israel/Palestine, Afghanistan, Sudan, and elsewhere. Council members should press for investigations of abuses by other countries in need of scrutiny, including major powers. These should include China’s crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and others in Xinjiang, as well as the US military’s unlawful strikes targeting vessels the Caribbean and Pacific, amounting to extrajudicial killings. The council should also explore possible action to support global justice in the face of a US assault on international accountability mechanisms. The US on October 9 imposed unjustified sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court. The US had previously sanctioned ICC officials, Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, and several prominent Palestinian human rights groups. “The human rights movement is under increasing attack by powerful governments, including established democracies,” Charbonneau said. “The Human Rights Council has done victims of human rights abuses a huge service with investigations that often deter governments and armed groups from committing violations. We need the council now more than ever.”
